prompt: How would you grow a retail lending book in a competitive market while protecting asset quality?
text:
Growing a retail book without compromising asset quality comes down to being selective about where you grow and disciplined about how you underwrite.

Start by identifying segments where you have a genuine edge, whether that is a geography you understand well, a customer profile your competitors underserve, or a product where your turnaround time is meaningfully better. Growth that relies only on cutting rates or loosening eligibility tends to attract the borrowers others have already rejected.

On the risk side, keep credit policy centralised even as sourcing expands. Use bureau data, bank statement analysis and early warning signals to monitor cohorts by vintage, so you can see within three to six months whether a new channel or product is performing as expected. Set clear limits on concentration by segment, ticket size and sourcing partner.

Finally, align incentives. If sales teams are paid only on disbursement volume, quality will suffer. Linking a portion of variable pay to early delinquency rates keeps growth and risk pulling in the same direction.

prompt: How should an NBFC manage its GNPA during an economic downturn?
text:
An economic downturn tests the resilience of an NBFC's credit processes more severely than any other phase of the cycle. The management of gross non-performing assets during such a period should therefore be approached as an integrated exercise spanning origination, portfolio monitoring, collections and provisioning, rather than as a narrow recovery function.

The first priority is the early identification of stress. Institutions should strengthen their early warning systems by tracking cheque and NACH bounce rates, bureau triggers, utilisation patterns and sector-level indicators, and should review the portfolio at a more granular level than usual. Accounts in the SMA-1 and SMA-2 categories warrant particular attention, since timely intervention at this stage is considerably more effective than recovery after classification as NPA.

Second, origination standards should be recalibrated in light of the changed environment. This may involve tightening eligibility for vulnerable segments, reducing loan-to-value ratios, and temporarily curtailing exposure to sectors that are disproportionately affected.

Third, the collections function must be adequately resourced. A segmented approach, in which borrowers facing temporary cash-flow disruption are distinguished from those exhibiting wilful default, allows the institution to deploy restructuring, where permitted under the regulatory framework, and enforcement action appropriately.

Finally, the institution should maintain conservative provisioning under its expected credit loss model, including management overlays where historical data does not adequately capture current conditions. Transparent communication with the board, lenders and rating agencies regarding asset quality trends will help preserve confidence and access to funding throughout the downturn.

prompt: Describe how your organisation handled the COVID-19 moratorium.
text:
When the RBI announced the moratorium on 27 March 2020, we had roughly 1,85,000 live retail accounts and an AUM of about ₹6,400 crore, most of it home loans and LAP to self-employed borrowers in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh. Within the first week, nearly 62% of our customers by value had either opted in or simply stopped paying, and our collections team, which was used to visiting customers physically, could not step out.

The first thing I did was set up a daily 8 a.m. call with the heads of risk, treasury, collections and operations. For the first six weeks, liquidity was the real worry, not credit. We had about ₹1,100 crore of debt repayments due over the next six months while inflows had nearly halved. We drew down undrawn bank lines early, slowed disbursements to almost zero in April, and kept around ₹1,500 crore in liquid investments, even though the negative carry cost us roughly 40 basis points of margin that year.

On the customer side, we decided to move from an opt-out to an opt-in moratorium in the second phase. Our call centre and branch staff phoned every customer to explain that interest would continue to accrue, and that it was better to pay if they could. By September 2020, moratorium usage had dropped to about 18% of the book.

When the moratorium ended, we segmented the book using bank statement data and repayment behaviour during the moratorium period. Customers with a temporary hit were offered restructuring under the Resolution Framework, and we restructured about 3.5% of AUM. We also made a management overlay of ₹95 crore under ECL in FY2020-21, which in hindsight was slightly more than we needed.

The biggest lesson for me was that trust matters more than policy in a crisis. Customers who had a relationship with their branch manager came back to paying far sooner than those who did not. That experience shaped how we built our collections model afterwards, with more emphasis on the relationship and less on the field visit as a pressure tactic.

prompt: What are the key risks in digital lending and how should lenders address them?
text:
Digital lending makes it easy to give loans quickly. That speed is useful, but it also creates new risks. I would group them into five areas.

The first is credit risk. In a digital journey, you often do not meet the borrower. You rely on bureau data, bank statements and phone data. Some of these signals look good at first but do not predict repayment well. New borrowers with thin credit files are hard to judge. The answer is to start with small loan amounts, watch how each group of borrowers repays, and only then increase limits. Lenders should also test their models often, not once a year. It helps to keep a human review for cases the model is unsure about.

The second is fraud. Fake identities, borrowed documents and organised fraud rings are common. A digital process can be attacked at scale. Lenders need strong identity checks, such as video KYC and checks against government databases. They should also look for patterns, like many applications from the same device or address.

The third is conduct risk. Some lending apps have used harsh recovery methods, hidden fees and misuse of customer contacts. This has hurt customers and damaged trust in the whole sector. The RBI's digital lending rules now require clear disclosure of the annual percentage rate, a key fact statement, and a cooling-off period. Money must go directly from the lender to the borrower's bank account. Lenders are responsible for what their partners do. So they must check their partners carefully and audit them.

The fourth is data and cyber risk. Digital lenders hold a lot of personal data. A data leak can harm customers and the lender's reputation. Lenders should collect only the data they need, take clear consent, store it safely in India, and test their systems for weak points. Staff access to customer data should be limited and logged.

The fifth is collection risk. Digital loans are often small and unsecured. When many borrowers stop paying at once, collections become hard. Lenders should plan for this before they grow. They need fair, polite reminder systems, trained collection staff and clear rules for any agency they use.

There is also a business risk. Many digital lenders depend on one partner for most of their customers. If that partner leaves, volumes drop sharply. It is safer to have more than one channel.

In short, digital lending works when the lender treats speed as a tool, not the goal. Good checks, fair treatment and steady testing matter more than how fast a loan is approved.

prompt: How do you retain talent in a high-attrition sales and collections workforce?
text:
Honestly, I don't think you ever 'solve' attrition in field sales and collections. You manage it. When I was running a cluster of branches in Rajasthan, we were losing something like 55-60% of our field staff every year, and for a while I treated it as a hiring problem. Hire faster, hire more. It didn't work. We were just refilling a leaky bucket.

What changed my thinking was an exit conversation with a collections officer in Bhilwara. He'd been with us about eight months, he was good, and he was leaving for a job that paid maybe ₹1,500 more a month. I asked him if it was really about the money. He laughed a bit and said no, it was that nobody had ever told him what he'd be doing in two years. His manager had changed three times in eight months. He didn't know who to complain to when his incentive was calculated wrong.

That stuck with me. A lot of what we call attrition is really people concluding, fairly reasonably, that nobody's paying attention to them.

So a few things we did. First, we fixed the boring stuff. Incentives got paid on time and the calculation was visible on their phones, so they weren't chasing the branch accountant every month. It sounds small. It wasn't. Disputes over incentives were one of the top reasons people left in the first six months.

Second, we stopped moving branch managers around so much. Stability at the first-line manager level mattered more than almost anything else. People don't quit companies, they quit the guy who shouts at them in the morning huddle, and if that guy keeps changing, there's no relationship at all.

Third, we made the first 90 days a lot less brutal. New joiners in collections were getting the worst buckets and the toughest geographies because nobody else wanted them. Naturally they burnt out. We started pairing them with an experienced colleague for the first month and giving them a mixed portfolio.

Fourth, and this one took longer, we built a visible path up. Field officer to senior officer to team lead to branch manager, with clear criteria. We promoted a few people from the field to branch manager within two to three years, and we made a point of talking about it. Nothing convinces a 24-year-old in Kota that there's a future here like seeing someone who sat in his chair two years ago now running the branch.

Pay matters, obviously. If you're 20% below market you'll lose people no matter what. But beyond a point, an extra few hundred rupees doesn't hold anyone. Respect, predictability and a sense of progress do.

Did attrition go to some magic low number? No. We got it down to around 35% over two years, which in that business is pretty decent. More importantly, the people we were losing were mostly the ones we'd have let go anyway, not the good ones.

prompt: Explain the co-lending model between banks and NBFCs and its strategic value.
text:
Co-lending, also called co-origination, is an arrangement wherein a bank and an NBFC jointly extend a loan to the borrower, with both entities taking a share of the exposure on their own books. The RBI formalised the Co-Lending Model (CLM) vide its circular of November 2020, which replaced the earlier co-origination framework of 2018. The original intent was to improve the flow of credit to the unserved and underserved sectors of the economy, especially priority sector segments, by combining the lower cost of funds of banks with the greater reach and origination capability of NBFCs.

Under the model, the NBFC sources the customer, does the initial underwriting and retains a minimum share of the loan on its own books, which was 20% under the 2020 framework. The bank takes the balance share. The bank can either have a prior irrevocable commitment to take its portion of all loans originated as per the agreed credit policy, or it can do its own due diligence on a case-to-case basis before taking its share. A single escrow account is maintained for disbursement and collections, and the interest rate charged to the customer is a blended rate. Grievance redressal, KYC and fair practices code requirements apply as per the norms of both the regulated entities. More recently, the RBI has widened the framework so that co-lending is no longer limited to priority sector loans and can happen between a broader set of regulated entities, with a lower minimum retention requirement, but the underlying logic remains the same.

Now coming to the strategic value. For the NBFC, the biggest benefit is access to low-cost funds without the full balance sheet burden. Since only a portion of the loan sits on the NBFC's book, it is able to grow AUM much faster than its own capital and borrowings would otherwise permit. This becomes a source of fee and spread income, as the NBFC typically earns the differential between the blended customer rate and the yield passed on to the bank. It also helps in improving return on equity, since the capital requirement is lesser.

For the bank, the model provides access to customers in Tier 2, Tier 3 and rural geographies where opening branches is not viable. It also helps the bank in meeting its priority sector lending targets, especially in sub-segments like small and marginal farmers, micro enterprises and weaker sections, where banks have historically fallen short and have had to invest in RIDF deposits with NABARD or buy PSLCs.

For the customer, the benefit is in terms of a more competitive interest rate than what a standalone NBFC would have offered, along with the convenience and doorstep service of an NBFC.

However, the model is not without its challenges. Technology integration between the bank and NBFC systems is a major hurdle, as both need to be on the same page for real-time approval, disbursement and collection. Many co-lending tie-ups in the initial phase did not take off for this very reason. There is also the issue of credit policy alignment, since banks are generally more conservative and may reject a good number of cases which the NBFC has already sanctioned. Further, the NBFC continues to carry reputational risk for the entire loan, since the customer sees the NBFC as the face of the lender, even though a majority of the money may be from the bank.

In my view, co-lending should be seen as a strategic lever and not merely a funding route. NBFCs which have strong origination capability, robust underwriting and a good technology stack are best placed to benefit from the same. Going forward, as the framework matures and API-based integration becomes standard, co-lending is expected to play a much larger role in taking formal credit to MSMEs and affordable housing customers in Bharat.

prompt: What role does data analytics play in credit decisioning?
text:
Data analytics has moved from being a supporting function in credit decisioning to sitting at the centre of it, particularly in retail and MSME lending, where volumes are high and ticket sizes are small.

At the origination stage, analytics allows lenders to build scorecards that combine bureau information with alternative data such as bank statement transactions, GST filings, utility payments and, with appropriate consent, data accessed through the Account Aggregator framework. This is especially valuable for thin-file or new-to-credit customers, who would otherwise be rejected or priced conservatively simply because there is little history to evaluate.

Analytics also improves consistency. A well-validated model applies the same logic to every application, reducing the variability that comes with purely manual underwriting, and frees experienced credit officers to focus on complex or borderline cases.

Beyond the approval decision, data supports limit setting, risk-based pricing, fraud detection and early warning systems that flag deterioration before an account becomes delinquent.

That said, models are only as good as the data and assumptions behind them. Lenders need regular back-testing, monitoring for drift, clear governance over model changes, and attention to explainability and fairness, so that decisions can be justified to customers, auditors and the regulator.

prompt: How should a lender approach risk-based pricing?
text:
Risk-based pricing rests on the principle that the interest rate charged to a borrower should reflect the cost of funds, operating expenses, expected credit losses and the cost of capital associated with that particular exposure, together with a reasonable return. Implemented well, it allows a lender to compete for lower-risk customers while being adequately compensated for higher-risk segments.

The foundation of any risk-based pricing framework is a reliable measure of risk. This generally requires a validated internal scorecard or rating model that combines bureau scores, income stability, loan-to-value ratio, collateral quality and product characteristics into an estimate of the probability of default. Loss given default should similarly be estimated by product and collateral type. Without these inputs, pricing differentiation becomes arbitrary.

The second element is a transparent cost build-up. The institution should determine its marginal cost of funds, the allocated operating cost per account, expected loss and the capital charge for each risk grade. The resulting rate grid should then be compared with prevailing market rates to assess competitive positioning.

Third, governance is essential. Pricing decisions should be approved by an appropriate committee, documented in a board-approved interest rate policy, and communicated clearly to customers. The Reserve Bank of India requires NBFCs to adopt such a policy, to disclose the rationale for charging different rates to different categories of borrowers, and to avoid charges that are excessive or usurious.

Finally, the framework should be reviewed periodically. Actual delinquency outcomes by pricing band should be monitored to confirm that higher-priced segments are in fact generating adequate risk-adjusted returns. Lenders should also guard against adverse selection, whereby pricing for higher-risk grades attracts precisely those borrowers whose risk exceeds what the model anticipates.

prompt: What is the most important leadership lesson you have learned in your career?
text:
The most important lesson I have learned is that the quality of decisions in an organisation depends far more on what people feel safe telling you than on how smart the leadership team is.

I learned this the hard way in FY2017-18. I was heading the retail business at a mid-sized housing finance company, and we were growing at about 35% a year. Disbursements had crossed ₹2,800 crore that year and the board was happy. What I did not know was that in two of our regions, the sourcing teams had been leaning heavily on a handful of DSAs, and some of those files had income documents that were, to put it politely, creative. Our regional credit managers had noticed. A couple of them had even raised it informally with their seniors. But the message that reached me had been diluted to the point of being meaningless, something like 'a few quality concerns being addressed locally.'

By the time the early delinquency numbers made the problem obvious, we had about ₹180 crore of loans from those channels on the book. Our 90+ DPD in that cohort went to nearly 9% within eighteen months, against 1.2% for the rest of the portfolio. We had to terminate eleven DSAs, take disciplinary action against several employees and make provisions that hurt our profit for two quarters.

When I went back and looked at how the information had moved, the issue was clear. People had been rewarded for growth and gently discouraged from being the ones to slow it down. Nobody had lied. They had simply learned what the organisation wanted to hear.

After that, I changed how I ran reviews. I started every monthly business review with credit and collections, not disbursements. I made it a practice to call two or three regional credit managers directly every month, without their bosses on the line, and ask what was bothering them. We set up a simple channel where anyone could flag a sourcing concern, and I made a point of publicly thanking the first few people who used it, even when the concern turned out to be minor.

None of this is sophisticated. But I am convinced that most large failures in lending are visible to someone in the organisation well before they show up in the numbers. A leader's real job is to make sure that person speaks up, and that someone listens when they do.

prompt: How can lenders solve the MSME credit gap in India?
text:
India has more than six crore small businesses. Most of them cannot get enough formal credit. Estimates of the gap vary, but they run into many lakh crore rupees. Many small business owners still borrow from moneylenders, suppliers or relatives at high rates. Closing this gap is hard, but there are clear steps lenders can take.

First, we need to understand why the gap exists. Most small businesses do not keep proper accounts. Many file income tax returns that show low income. Some are not registered at all. They often do not have property to give as security. For a lender, this makes it hard to judge whether the business can repay. The cost of checking a small loan is also high compared to the interest it earns. So lenders either say no or ask for collateral the owner does not have.

Second, lenders should use the data that small businesses do have. GST returns show sales. Bank statements show cash coming in and going out. UPI payments leave a clear record. Through the Account Aggregator system, a lender can see this data with the owner's consent. This helps judge a business even when it has no formal financial statements.

Third, lenders should design products that fit how small businesses work. A shop owner may need money for stock before a festival and repay it after. A fixed monthly EMI may not suit him. Short-term credit lines, loans linked to invoices, and repayment that matches cash flows work better.

Fourth, the cost of giving each loan must come down. This means simple forms, digital checks, and quick decisions for small amounts. A ₹3 lakh loan cannot carry the same paperwork as a ₹3 crore loan.

Fifth, lenders should use the support that already exists. The CGTMSE scheme gives guarantees on loans to small businesses without collateral. This reduces the lender's loss if the loan goes bad. Co-lending between banks and NBFCs lets the bank's low-cost money reach customers through the NBFC's local presence. TReDS platforms let small suppliers get paid early against bills raised on large buyers.

Sixth, lenders need people on the ground. Data helps, but in smaller towns, a loan officer who knows the local market can spot good and bad borrowers better than any model. The best results come from mixing both.

Finally, lenders must be patient. Small business loans will see higher losses in the early years. A lender that builds data over time will get better at pricing the risk. One that gives up after one bad year will never learn.

The gap will not close quickly. But with better use of data, simple products, and support from guarantee schemes, lenders can reach many more small businesses safely and profitably.

prompt: How do you build trust with customers in a market where lenders have a poor reputation?
text:
I'll start with something a customer told me years ago in a village outside Nashik, because it's stayed with me. We were doing a small home improvement loan for a family, maybe ₹2 lakh, and the husband asked our officer, quite seriously, how much he'd have to pay 'under the table' to get it sanctioned. He wasn't trying to bribe us. He just assumed that's how it worked, because that's how it had worked every other time he'd dealt with a lender or a government office.

That's the starting point in a lot of markets. People don't trust lenders, and they've got reasons. Somebody in the village took a loan and got harassed by recovery agents. Somebody signed papers they couldn't read and found out later about charges nobody mentioned. Somebody's cousin paid a 'file charge' to an agent who disappeared. You're not starting from zero. You're starting from minus.

So what actually works? In my experience, it's mostly unglamorous.

Be boringly clear about money. Tell people the full cost, in rupees, not just a rate. 'You'll pay ₹4,350 every month for five years, and in total that's about ₹2,61,000' lands very differently from '14.5% reducing.' Put it on one page, in Marathi or Hindi or whatever they read, and make the officer walk them through it. The RBI's key fact statement rules have helped here, but you can do better than the minimum.

Don't let anyone collect cash informally. This is a big one. In our business, we made it a sackable offence for an employee to take any payment that wasn't receipted through the system, and we told customers that, over and over. Fraud by staff or agents is one of the fastest ways to lose a whole village.

Be decent when things go wrong. This is where reputations really get made. When a customer misses an EMI because the crop failed or someone in the family is in hospital, how your collections team behaves will be talked about for years. We trained our people to ask first and push later. Not every case gets a concession, obviously. But the tone matters enormously.

Show up consistently. Same officer, same branch, same phone number that actually gets answered. In smaller towns, the relationship is with the person, not the brand. If you churn your staff every six months, you're asking customers to trust a stranger again and again.

And fix complaints fast and visibly. When a customer has been wrongly charged, refund it and say sorry. Don't make them fight for it. Word spreads in a small community, and one resolved complaint often brings in more business than a hoarding on the highway.

The funny thing is, none of this is new. Good moneylenders and good cooperative banks have done it for generations. What's different now is that we've got tools to do it at scale: SMS confirmations for every payment, WhatsApp statements, call recordings for collections. Those help. But the tools only work if the behaviour behind them is right.

That family in Nashik, by the way, repaid in full and came back a few years later for a bigger loan to build a second floor. He brought his brother along too. That's really how trust spreads.

prompt: How has RBI's scale-based regulation framework changed the way NBFCs operate?
text:
The Scale Based Regulation (SBR) framework, issued by the Reserve Bank of India in October 2021 and made effective from October 2022, is in my view the most significant change in the regulatory architecture for NBFCs in the last two decades. Prior to the same, NBFCs were broadly regulated on the basis of whether they were deposit-taking or not and whether they were systemically important, with an asset size threshold of ₹500 crore. The IL&FS and DHFL episodes clearly brought out that this approach was not sufficient, since some very large NBFCs had become interconnected with the banking system and capital markets to an extent that their failure could impact financial stability.

Under SBR, NBFCs have been placed in four layers, namely the Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer and a Top Layer which is ideally expected to remain empty. The Base Layer consists of smaller non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size below ₹1,000 crore. The Middle Layer includes all deposit-taking NBFCs, non-deposit taking NBFCs with assets of ₹1,000 crore and above, and certain categories like HFCs, IFCs and core investment companies. The Upper Layer comprises those NBFCs specifically identified by the RBI on the basis of size, interconnectedness, complexity and other parameters, and the list is reviewed annually. The regulatory intensity increases as one moves up the layers.

Now, coming to how this has changed the way NBFCs operate, I would like to highlight a few key areas.

Firstly, governance standards have been considerably raised. Middle and Upper Layer NBFCs are now required to have a Chief Compliance Officer, a board-approved compliance policy, and a proper compensation policy. Independent directors are restricted from serving on the boards of too many NBFCs at the same time, and Upper Layer NBFCs must get listed within three years of identification. Senior management compensation is also required to have malus and clawback arrangements, which has brought a much stronger alignment between risk-taking and reward.

Secondly, the NPA recognition norm for NBFCs has been brought closer to banks. The classification period has been progressively tightened from 180 days overdue to 90 days overdue, as per a glide path ending in March 2026. This has had a direct impact on reported GNPA numbers, and many NBFCs had to strengthen their collections infrastructure in the early buckets so as to avoid slippages.

Thirdly, Upper Layer NBFCs are required to maintain Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 9%, and there are differential standard asset provisioning requirements. Large exposure framework norms similar to banks also apply to them. This has made capital planning and concentration management a board-level agenda item.

Fourthly, there are new restrictions on loans to directors, senior officers and their relatives, along with ceilings on IPO financing and certain restrictions on financing land acquisition. Disclosure requirements in the annual financial statements have also been significantly expanded, covering exposures, related party transactions and customer complaints.

The direction of travel is quite clear: larger NBFCs are expected to look and behave more like banks in terms of governance and risk management.

From an operational perspective, the impact has been felt mostly in terms of compliance cost, the need for better technology and data systems, and a change in board culture. Many promoter-driven NBFCs which were used to a more informal style of functioning have had to professionalise quickly. At the same time, it has improved the overall credibility of the sector with banks, mutual funds and rating agencies, which in turn helps in raising funds.

To conclude, SBR is a proportionate framework. It allows smaller NBFCs to retain their flexibility, while ensuring that the systemically large ones are held to a standard commensurate with the risk they pose. Those NBFCs which have embraced the spirit of the same, and not merely complied in letter, are today better positioned for sustainable growth.

prompt: How do you build a strong risk culture across an organisation?
text:
A strong risk culture is less about policies and more about how people behave when no one is checking. Most lending organisations have detailed credit manuals; the difference lies in whether staff at every level treat risk as part of their job or as someone else's problem.

It starts with the tone at the top. If senior leaders celebrate disbursement numbers while treating credit concerns as obstacles, employees quickly learn what really matters. Leaders need to visibly back risk teams when they slow down a deal for good reasons, and discuss asset quality with the same energy as growth.

Second, accountability has to be shared. Business teams should own the quality of what they originate, not just the volume. Linking a portion of incentives to portfolio performance, such as early delinquency or bounce rates on sourced loans, makes this concrete.

Third, people need to feel safe raising concerns. A whistle-blower policy is necessary but not sufficient. Managers should actively ask frontline staff what they are seeing and respond constructively, even when the news is unwelcome.

Fourth, invest in capability. Regular training on fraud patterns, regulatory requirements and case studies of past losses helps employees recognise risk in their daily work.

Finally, reinforce the culture through consequences. Breaches of policy should be handled consistently, regardless of how senior or high-performing the individual is. Nothing undermines a risk culture faster than visible exceptions for star performers.

prompt: What is the role of the Chief Risk Officer, and how should the CRO interact with the business?
text:
The Chief Risk Officer is responsible for ensuring that the institution identifies, measures, monitors and manages the risks inherent in its business in a manner consistent with the risk appetite approved by the board. In the context of an Indian NBFC, this encompasses credit risk, market and liquidity risk, operational risk, including fraud and information security, as well as compliance and reputational risk.

The Reserve Bank of India has emphasised the independence of this function. Its guidelines for NBFCs above a specified asset size require the CRO to be appointed for a fixed tenure with board approval, to report to the Managing Director and the Risk Management Committee of the board, and to have no business targets. The CRO may be removed before the end of the tenure only with board approval, and such removal must be reported to the regulator. These provisions are designed to ensure that the CRO can express an independent view without fear of consequences.

Independence, however, should not be confused with isolation. An effective CRO engages closely with business heads during product design, policy formulation and strategic planning, rather than reviewing proposals only after they have been developed. Early involvement allows risk considerations to shape a product from the outset, which is considerably more efficient than rejecting a fully formed proposal at a late stage.

The relationship is best characterised as one of constructive challenge. The business is responsible for generating growth and owning the risks it originates; the CRO is responsible for ensuring that those risks are understood, appropriately priced and contained within approved limits. Disagreements are natural and, indeed, healthy. Where they cannot be resolved, there should be a clear escalation path to the Managing Director and, where necessary, to the Risk Management Committee.

The CRO should also contribute to the institution's forward-looking thinking through stress testing, portfolio analytics and early warning frameworks. In this capacity, the function moves beyond compliance and becomes a genuine partner in strategy, helping the organisation pursue growth opportunities with a clear understanding of the downside.

prompt: Reflect on a failure in your career and what you learned from it.
text:
The failure I think about most is our unsecured business loan product, which I championed in FY2018-19.

At the time, I was the business head for MSME lending at an NBFC with an AUM of roughly ₹9,000 crore, almost entirely secured LAP. Our yields were coming under pressure because banks had become aggressive in the ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore LAP segment. I made the case to the board that we should launch unsecured business loans of ₹5 lakh to ₹30 lakh to our existing LAP customers and to similar profiles sourced through our DSAs, at yields of 18-21% against the 11-12% we were earning on LAP. The numbers on paper were compelling. I projected a ₹1,200 crore book in three years with credit costs of about 3%.

We launched in eight cities in July 2018. By March 2019, we had disbursed close to ₹450 crore. Then the problems started. The NBFC liquidity crisis after IL&FS meant many of our customers' own suppliers and buyers were stretched. Our underwriting, which had borrowed heavily from our LAP playbook, had not properly accounted for the fact that without collateral, the customer's incentive to prioritise our EMI was much weaker. The 90+ DPD on the product touched 7.8% by December 2019, and then COVID came. We eventually wrote off or provided for about ₹110 crore on that book, and we stopped fresh sourcing in 2020.

Looking back, three things went wrong, and they were mostly my responsibility.

First, I mistook a yield problem for a product opportunity. We were reacting to margin pressure rather than to a real customer need or a capability we had. Second, we scaled too quickly. Eight cities in the first year was ambitious. If we had piloted in two cities with a strict cap of ₹50 crore and waited for at least twelve months of performance data, we would have seen the stress before it became large. Third, I did not listen carefully enough to our credit head, who had argued for separate scorecards and a dedicated collections team for unsecured lending. I treated that as caution rather than as expertise.

What I took away was a simple discipline that I still follow. For any new product, I now ask three questions before approving a launch: do we have a genuine edge in serving this customer, what is the maximum we are prepared to lose while we learn, and who in the room disagrees and why? I also insist that the pilot phase has a hard rupee cap and a defined review date. It slows things down a little, but it has saved us from repeating that mistake.

prompt: Walk us through how you would launch a new loan product.
text:
I would launch a new loan product in clear stages. Each stage has a simple goal. I would not move to the next stage until the current one is done well.

The first stage is to understand the customer. Who is the product for? What do they need the money for? How do they earn, and when do they get paid? What are they using today, and why is it not good enough? I would talk to real customers, branch staff and collection teams before writing any policy. Many products fail because they are built around what the lender wants to sell, not what the customer needs.

The second stage is to check if we can do it well. Do we have the right people? Can our systems handle it? Do we know how to judge the risk? Is it allowed under RBI rules and our own board policies? If the answer to any of these is no, we either fix it first or drop the idea.

The third stage is to design the product. This means setting the loan amount, tenure, interest rate, fees, and who is eligible. It also means writing the credit policy and the collection plan. I would ask the risk team to estimate the likely losses and make sure the price covers them, along with our cost of funds and operating costs. I would keep the product simple. A customer should be able to understand it in a few minutes.

The fourth stage is approvals and setup. The product needs sign-off from the credit committee and, where needed, the board. Legal and compliance must check the loan agreement and the key fact statement. The technology team must set up the product in the loan system. Staff must be trained on how to sell it, how to check documents and how to explain the terms.

The fifth stage is a pilot. I would start in two or three branches only. I would set a limit on how much we will lend in the pilot, for example ₹20 crore. During the pilot, I would watch a few things closely: approval rates, time taken to disburse, customer complaints, and most of all, how the first few EMIs are paid. Early bounces tell you a lot.

The sixth stage is review. After about six to nine months, I would look at the data with the risk, sales and collection teams. What worked? What went wrong? Were our loss estimates right? Do we need to change the policy or the price? This is the point to make changes, while the book is still small.

The last stage is scale-up. If the pilot results are good, we expand to more branches in steps. We keep tracking the same numbers. If problems appear, we slow down.

The main idea is simple. Go slowly at the start, learn fast, and only grow once you are sure the product works for both the customer and the company. It is much cheaper to fix a small mistake than a large one.

prompt: If you could start your career again, what would you do differently?
text:
Funny question, because I actually get asked this by younger colleagues fairly often, usually over chai after some long review meeting. My answer's changed a bit over the years.

When I was younger I'd have said something about wanting to move faster. I started as a management trainee in a bank's retail assets team in the early 2000s, and I spent nearly four years in credit processing and operations before I got anywhere near a business role. At the time I was impatient. My batchmates were jumping to private banks and foreign banks for 40-50% hikes, and I stayed put. I used to think that was a mistake.

Now I think it's probably the best thing that happened to me. Those years in operations meant I knew exactly how a loan file moved, where documents got lost, which steps were pointless and which ones actually caught fraud. Later, when I was running businesses, I could smell a bad process from a mile off. A lot of senior people in lending have never actually sat with a disbursement team at 7 p.m. on the last day of the quarter. You can tell.

So I wouldn't change that. What I would change is mostly about people.

I'd have invested in relationships a lot earlier. I was quite transactional in my twenties and early thirties. Good at my job, did what was asked, didn't really bother with people who weren't directly useful. That was dumb. The industry in India is small. The credit manager you were short with in 2008 is the CRO of your biggest co-lending partner in 2020. I learned that one the slightly embarrassing way, sitting across a table from someone who clearly remembered.

I'd also have asked for feedback more, and taken it less personally. For a long time I had a reputation as someone who was sharp but hard to work for. Nobody told me directly. I found out in a 360-degree exercise when I was already a regional head, and it stung. One comment said something like 'He makes you feel stupid for asking questions.' I hadn't meant to, but I can see now that I did. If someone had told me that at 28, I'd have saved my teams a fair amount of grief.

The third thing is health. Lending is a 24/7 business when things go wrong, and I spent a lot of my forties not sleeping properly, eating at odd hours, travelling to branches every week. I'm fine, touch wood, but I know a few people from my generation who weren't so lucky. I'd have built some routine around exercise much earlier and protected it the way I protected board meetings.

And I'd probably have taken one big risk earlier. I had a chance to join a small NBFC as part of the founding team around 2011 and I didn't, mostly because of the home loan EMI and a new baby. That company did very well. I don't regret it exactly, my family needed the stability. But I do sometimes wonder.

If I had to boil it down for someone starting out now, I'd say: learn the plumbing of the business properly, be nicer to people than you think you need to be, look after your body, and don't let fear make all your decisions for you. The rest mostly takes care of itself.

prompt: How should a lender handle grievance redressal and the RBI Ombudsman?
text:
Grievance redressal is not merely a compliance requirement; it is a direct reflection of how the lender values its customers. Every NBFC is required to have a board-approved grievance redressal policy, a designated Grievance Redressal Officer whose details are displayed at all branches and on the website, and a clear escalation matrix.

The RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 covers NBFCs, and a customer can approach the Ombudsman if the complaint is not resolved within 30 days or if he is not satisfied with the reply. Hence it is in the interest of the lender to resolve the same at the first level itself.

In practice, lenders should track complaints by category and root cause, carry out monthly reviews at senior management level, and place a summary before the board. Root cause analysis of repeat complaints should also be carried out. Larger NBFCs are also required to appoint an Internal Ombudsman. Kindly note that a high volume of Ombudsman complaints invites supervisory attention, so prevention is always better than cure.

prompt: Describe your approach to mortgage underwriting for self-employed borrowers with informal income.
text:
Underwriting self-employed borrowers with informal income is one of the more challenging areas in Indian mortgage lending, because the income documented in tax returns often understates the true earning capacity of the business. A purely document-based approach would reject a large share of creditworthy customers, while an overly lenient approach invites significant risk. The answer lies in assessing cash flows carefully and building in adequate safeguards.

The core of the approach is a field-based income assessment. A trained credit officer visits the business, observes the scale of operations, checks stock levels, speaks with the owner about suppliers and customers, and reconstructs a realistic estimate of monthly income. This assessment is then triangulated against available evidence such as bank statements, GST returns, utility bills and, where available, data obtained through the Account Aggregator framework.

Bank statement analysis is particularly useful. Regular credits, the pattern of cash deposits, average balances and the presence of cheque bounces all provide insight into the stability of the business. Bureau history, even if limited to small loans or credit cards, gives an indication of repayment behaviour.

Given the higher uncertainty, lenders typically apply more conservative parameters for this segment. This may include a lower loan-to-value ratio, a lower fixed obligation to income ratio, a stronger emphasis on property title and marketability, and a co-applicant from the family.

Finally, it is important to monitor the performance of this segment separately. Tracking delinquency by income assessment method and by credit officer helps identify whether the assessments are reliable and where training or policy changes are needed. Done well, this segment can deliver attractive yields with manageable credit costs.

prompt: What is the role of the board's Risk Management Committee in an NBFC?
text:
The Risk Management Committee of the board serves as the principal forum through which the board discharges its oversight responsibility for the institution's risk profile. While the board as a whole remains ultimately accountable, the complexity and technical nature of risk management in a lending institution make it necessary to delegate detailed oversight to a dedicated committee with appropriate expertise.

The committee's foremost responsibility is to recommend the institution's risk appetite framework to the board and to monitor adherence to it. This framework should articulate, in both qualitative and quantitative terms, the level and types of risk the institution is prepared to accept in pursuit of its strategic objectives, including limits on asset quality, concentration, liquidity, capital adequacy and operational losses.

Second, the committee oversees the integrated risk management framework. It reviews the policies governing credit, market, liquidity, operational and compliance risk, evaluates the adequacy of the methodologies used to measure these risks, and examines the results of stress tests and scenario analyses. In the Indian context, the committee should also review the liquidity risk management framework, including compliance with the liquidity coverage ratio where applicable, and the institution's preparedness for adverse funding conditions.

Third, the committee provides oversight of the Chief Risk Officer. Under the Reserve Bank of India's guidelines, the CRO reports to the committee, and any premature removal or transfer requires board approval. The committee should meet the CRO periodically, including without the presence of executive management, so that concerns may be raised candidly.

Fourth, the committee should monitor emerging risks that may not yet be reflected in historical data, such as regulatory changes, technological disruption, climate-related risks and cybersecurity threats.

The effectiveness of the committee depends substantially on its composition and on the quality of the information it receives. Members should possess relevant expertise in banking, finance or risk management, and the agenda should allow sufficient time for substantive discussion rather than a mechanical review of reports. Management, for its part, should present information that is concise, forward-looking and candid about areas of concern. A committee that receives only reassurance is unlikely to be in a position to provide genuine oversight.

prompt: What would you prioritise in your first 100 days as head of retail lending?
text:
When I took over as head of retail lending at our NBFC in April 2022, the business had a book of about ₹14,500 crore across home loans, LAP and used vehicle finance, with 210 branches, mostly in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns in North and West India. GNPA was 3.9%, cost-to-income was around 47%, and disbursement growth had been flat for two years. I had a mandate from the MD to get growth back without letting asset quality slip. Here is roughly how I spent the first 100 days.

The first month was almost entirely listening. I visited 34 branches across eight states, and in each one I asked the same three questions: what is stopping you from disbursing more good loans, what are you worried about in your portfolio, and what would you change if you were in my chair? I also sat in on credit committee meetings and listened to recorded collection calls. By the end of the month, I had a fairly clear picture. Our turnaround time from login to sanction for home loans was 19 days, against 8 to 10 days for the better competitors. DSAs were taking their good files elsewhere and bringing us the leftovers.

In the second month, I focused on a small number of quick fixes. We cut out two redundant approval levels for loans below ₹25 lakh, moved legal and technical vendor assignment to a system-based allocation, and set a target of 10 days for TAT. We also sat down with our top 40 DSAs, who accounted for about 55% of sourcing, and gave them a single point of contact in each region. Within six weeks, TAT came down to 12 days and DSA logins went up by about 18%.

The third month was about the longer-term agenda. I worked with the CRO to separate our scorecards for salaried and self-employed customers, which had been combined, and to set up a monthly vintage review that the business and risk teams attended together. I also restructured the sales incentive so that 25% of the payout depended on the 12-month bounce rate of the files each person sourced.

Alongside this, I spent time on people. I replaced two regional heads who were not on board with the changes, and promoted three people from within who had strong credibility in the field. I also started a fortnightly town hall over video for all branch managers.

Looking back, the most important thing in the first 100 days was not any single initiative. It was establishing a few clear priorities, showing early results so people believed the changes were real, and building trust with the risk team so that growth and quality were seen as a shared goal. By the end of FY2022-23, disbursements were up 31% and GNPA had come down to 3.1%.

prompt: Explain the importance of asset-liability management for an NBFC.
text:
Asset-liability management, or ALM, is about making sure a lender has money coming in at the right time to pay what it owes. It sounds simple. In practice, getting it wrong has brought down large companies.

An NBFC lends money and borrows money. Its loans are its assets. Its borrowings are its liabilities. The problem is that these often do not match. A home loan may run for 15 or 20 years. But the NBFC may have borrowed that money from banks for 3 to 5 years, or from mutual funds for 3 months through commercial paper. So the NBFC must keep borrowing again and again to fund loans that will take many years to come back.

This works fine when markets are calm. Lenders are happy to roll over the debt. But when there is a shock, they may refuse. Then the NBFC has payments to make and not enough cash. It may be a healthy company with good loans, but it still cannot pay on time. This is a liquidity crisis. In 2018, after IL&FS defaulted, many NBFCs faced exactly this. Mutual funds stopped buying their short-term paper. Some NBFCs that relied heavily on such funding were badly hit, and a few never recovered.

ALM helps prevent this. There are three main parts.

The first is liquidity. The NBFC lists all the cash it expects to receive and pay in different time periods, such as the next 7 days, 14 days, one month, three months, and so on. If outflows are much larger than inflows in the short periods, that is a warning sign. The RBI sets limits on how big this gap can be in the short-term buckets. Larger NBFCs must also keep enough high-quality liquid assets, like government securities, to cover 30 days of stressed outflows. This is called the liquidity coverage ratio.

The second is interest rate risk. If an NBFC lends at fixed rates but borrows at floating rates, a rise in interest rates will cut its margin. ALM looks at how much the company's earnings and value would change if rates move, and tries to keep this within limits.

The third is funding mix. An NBFC should not depend too much on one type of lender or one type of borrowing. It should have a mix of bank loans, bonds, securitisation and other sources, with different maturity dates. It should also keep some unused bank credit lines for emergencies.

Who looks after ALM? Every NBFC has an Asset Liability Committee, usually called ALCO. It includes the CEO, CFO, treasury head and risk head. It meets regularly, looks at the gaps and risks, and decides what to do. The board also reviews ALM through its risk committee.

Good ALM costs money. Keeping extra cash or borrowing for longer periods is more expensive than short-term funding. This reduces profit a little in good times. But it is like insurance. When the market turns, a company with strong ALM keeps lending while others struggle to survive. That is why lenders, rating agencies and the RBI pay close attention to it. For an NBFC, it is not a back-office task. It is a question of survival.

prompt: What collections strategy would you adopt for a portfolio showing rising early-bucket delinquencies?
text:
First thing I'd do is not panic, and second thing is figure out whether it's really a collections problem at all. In my experience, when early buckets start rising, people jump straight to 'add more callers, add more field staff.' Sometimes that's right. Often the problem started six months earlier, at sourcing, and collections is just where it shows up.

So I'd start by cutting the data. Which months were these loans disbursed in? Which branches, which DSAs, which products, which customer segments? Are the bounces coming from first-EMI or second-EMI defaults, which smells like fraud or bad sourcing, or are they from older accounts that were paying fine and then stopped, which points to something going on with customers' incomes? I remember one portfolio, a two-wheeler book in eastern UP, where 0-30 bounces jumped from about 9% to 14% in a quarter. Everybody assumed it was the local economy. When we actually looked, nearly half the increase was from just three dealers, and a lot of those customers had never paid a single EMI. That's not a collections issue. That's a sourcing issue with a collections symptom.

Assuming you've sorted out the sourcing side, or it's genuinely customer stress, then yes, collections needs to step up. A few things I'd focus on.

Get in early. The cheapest money you'll ever collect is in the first few days after a bounce. Pre-due reminders, SMS and WhatsApp a few days before the EMI date, a call on the day of the bounce. A lot of customers in the 1-30 bucket aren't bad borrowers. They forgot, or salary came late, or the account didn't have enough balance on that particular day. A polite nudge fixes most of those.

Segment properly. Not everybody in the same bucket needs the same treatment. You can usually split it into people who'll self-cure with a reminder, people who need a proper conversation, and people who are going to be hard. Put your expensive field resources on the last two. Sending a field officer to someone who'd have paid after an SMS is just wasted money. We built a simple score using past payment behaviour, bounce history and bureau data. It wasn't fancy, but it cut our field visits by about a third with no drop in resolution.

Fix the payment friction. You'd be amazed how many customers want to pay and find it annoying to do so. Make UPI links work, let them pay at the branch, let the field officer take a digital payment on the spot with an instant receipt. And re-present NACH smartly, closer to salary dates if you can.

Watch the incentives and the behaviour. When delinquencies rise, there's pressure, and pressure is when you see agents cross lines. Threatening calls, calls to relatives, visits at odd hours. It's against RBI's guidelines, it's wrong, and in the age of social media it'll blow up in your face. Call recordings, regular audits, zero tolerance. I've let go of agencies with good resolution numbers because of how they got them.

Restructure where it makes sense. For customers with a real, temporary problem, a small change in EMI or a short deferment can save the account. Better a slightly delayed recovery than a hard write-off.

And keep the feedback loop going back to credit. Every month, collections should be telling the credit and sales teams what they're seeing. Which profiles are struggling, which documents turned out to be fake, which areas are stressed. That's how you stop the next wave rather than just mopping up this one.

It's not glamorous work. But the lenders who do well over a full cycle are almost always the ones who take early buckets seriously.

prompt: What is your view on affordable housing and the PMAY scheme for HFCs?
text:
Affordable housing is, in my opinion, one of the most important growth opportunities for HFCs in India over the coming decade. As per various estimates, the urban housing shortage itself is in the range of 1 to 2 crore units, the majority of which pertains to EWS and LIG households. These customers are largely self-employed or employed in the informal sector, and hence are not served adequately by banks.

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana played a very important role in this regard. Under the Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme, eligible beneficiaries received an interest subsidy upfront, which reduced their effective EMI substantially. HFCs having a strong presence in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns benefitted considerably, since PMAY gave customers a good reason to approach a formal lender. With PMAY-Urban 2.0, the government has continued the interest subsidy support in a modified form.

However, HFCs must keep in mind that a subsidy is not a substitute for proper underwriting. The same discipline in income assessment, legal and technical verification and collections is required. Lenders who did the needful on this front have built quality affordable housing books with low GNPA, while those who chased volumes only have faced difficulties subsequently.

prompt: Apply Porter's Five Forces to the Indian affordable housing finance market.
text:
Porter's Five Forces is a useful lens for understanding why the Indian affordable housing finance market has attracted so many entrants, and why profitability varies so widely among them.

Threat of new entrants: moderate to high. Regulatory barriers exist, since HFCs need registration and must meet capital requirements, but these are not prohibitive. Over the past decade, a number of new affordable HFCs have been set up with private equity backing, and small finance banks and larger NBFCs have also entered the segment. However, the real barriers are less visible: building a distribution network in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns, developing the ability to assess informal incomes, and accumulating a track record that allows access to low-cost funding. These take years to build.

Bargaining power of buyers: moderate. Individual borrowers in this segment have limited negotiating power, and many have few alternatives. However, as competition has increased, customers with stronger profiles are able to compare offers and move to banks through balance transfers once they have built a repayment history.

Bargaining power of suppliers: high. For a lender, the critical supplier is capital. Affordable HFCs depend on banks, NHB refinance, debt capital markets and securitisation. Their cost of funds is structurally higher than that of banks, and funding conditions can tighten quickly, as the period after the IL&FS default showed.

Threat of substitutes: moderate. Substitutes include informal borrowing, chit funds and self-financed incremental construction, which remains common in smaller towns. For salaried borrowers with good documentation, bank home loans are a close substitute.

Competitive rivalry: high and rising. Banks have moved down-market, particularly for salaried customers, and pricing pressure is significant. Differentiation tends to come from turnaround time, an understanding of customer cash flows and local presence rather than from price.

Taken together, the analysis suggests that sustainable advantage in this market comes from operating efficiency, underwriting skill for informal income profiles, and diversified, stable funding. Players that compete primarily on price against banks are likely to find returns under pressure, while those that build depth in underserved segments can earn attractive risk-adjusted returns.

prompt: How should a lending institution allocate capital across business lines?
text:
Capital allocation is among the most consequential decisions taken by the leadership of a lending institution, since it determines not only the shape of the balance sheet but also the risk profile and long-term return on equity of the enterprise. An effective framework should be explicit, analytically grounded and subject to regular review by the board.

The starting point is a consistent measure of the capital consumed by each business line. Regulatory capital, computed on the basis of risk weights prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India, provides one perspective. However, regulatory risk weights are relatively coarse; for instance, the November 2023 increase in risk weights on consumer credit applied broadly across unsecured personal loans regardless of the underlying risk of individual portfolios. Institutions are therefore well advised to supplement regulatory measures with an internal assessment of economic capital, derived from estimates of expected and unexpected losses, concentration risk and stress scenarios.

Having established the capital consumed by each business, the institution should evaluate the risk-adjusted return generated on that capital. A measure such as risk-adjusted return on capital, which accounts for yield, cost of funds, operating expenses, expected credit losses and the capital charge, permits a like-for-like comparison between, for example, a secured home loan portfolio with modest yields and an unsecured personal loan portfolio with high yields and correspondingly high losses.

Return, however, should not be the sole criterion. Strategic considerations carry significant weight. A business line may generate below-average returns in the near term but provide diversification benefits, access to a customer base with cross-sell potential, or a foothold in a segment expected to grow substantially. Conversely, a highly profitable business may carry concentration, regulatory or reputational risks that warrant restraint.

The allocation process should be integrated with the institution's annual business planning and its Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process. Each business head should present a capital plan setting out expected growth, returns and risk, and these plans should be reconciled against the institution's overall capital position, including a buffer for stress conditions and any planned capital raising.

Finally, allocations should be monitored and revisited. Actual performance should be compared with plan on a quarterly basis, and capital should be redirected where a business persistently fails to meet its hurdle rate without a compelling strategic justification. Such discipline ensures that capital, which is both scarce and costly, is deployed where it creates the greatest sustainable value for shareholders and other stakeholders.

prompt: Case study: A mid-sized HFC's GNPA has risen from 2.1% to 4.8% in 18 months. What would you do as the new CEO?
text:
I have been in a version of this situation, so let me answer partly from that experience. In 2019 I joined an HFC with an AUM of about ₹7,200 crore where GNPA had moved from 1.9% to 4.4% over roughly the same period. The playbook I followed there would be my starting point here.

My first 30 days would be about diagnosis, not action. A rise from 2.1% to 4.8% is large enough that it is unlikely to be one thing. I would want the book cut by disbursement vintage, product, state, branch, sourcing channel, ticket size and customer profile. In my earlier case, about 60% of the incremental NPAs came from LAP loans above ₹50 lakh sourced in a 14-month window through a handful of DSAs in two states. The rest was spread more evenly and was linked to the general stress among small traders after demonetisation and GST. Those two problems needed very different responses.

Second, I would stop the bleeding at the front end. Any cohort that is clearly underperforming would see sourcing paused or the policy tightened immediately, even if it costs growth for a few quarters. In 2019, we suspended 23 DSAs, brought the maximum LTV on LAP down from 65% to 55%, and moved the self-employed income assessment for tickets above ₹30 lakh to a central team.

Third, I would rebuild collections around the buckets. Early buckets need high-volume, well-segmented tele-calling and field follow-up. The NPA book needs a separate legal and recovery team, using SARFAESI where the security is good. We set up a dedicated recovery vertical of about 80 people, and within 18 months recoveries from the NPA pool went from roughly ₹15 crore a quarter to ₹45 crore a quarter. Some of the harder accounts we sold to an ARC at about 38% of principal outstanding, which freed up management bandwidth.

Fourth, I would be honest with the board, lenders and rating agencies. I would take a clean-up provision in the first year rather than drip-feeding bad news. We increased our provision coverage on Stage 3 from 28% to 41% in my first year. Profit fell sharply, but our lenders told me later that the transparency was the reason they kept their lines open.

Fifth, I would look at people and incentives. A GNPA spike of this kind is usually accompanied by sales incentives tied purely to volume and a credit team that has been overruled too often. I would strengthen the CRO's role and make credit approvals independent of business reporting lines.

In my case, GNPA peaked at 5.2% and came down to 2.6% about two and a half years later, while AUM grew modestly. It was not quick, and it required patience from the board. But I would follow the same sequence again: understand the problem precisely, stop new damage, recover what you can, and fix the incentives that caused it in the first place.

prompt: Describe the role of credit bureaus and how you use bureau data.
text:
A credit bureau is a company that collects information on how people and businesses repay their loans. In India, there are four bureaus licensed by the RBI: TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, Equifax and CRIF High Mark. Every bank and NBFC must report its borrowers' data to all four, now every fortnight. The bureaus then share this data with lenders when a customer applies for a loan.

The main thing a bureau report shows is a person's loan history. It lists all their current and past loans and credit cards. For each one, it shows the amount, the lender, the date it was taken and how it was repaid month by month. If the person missed payments, the report shows how many days late they were. It also lists recent loan enquiries, which tell you if the person has been applying to many lenders. Most reports also include a score, usually between 300 and 900. A higher score means lower risk.

We use bureau data at almost every stage of the loan.

Before we approve a loan, the bureau report is one of the first things we check. If someone has a recent default, a write-off or a settlement, we usually decline or ask for strong reasons. If the person already has many loans, we check whether they can afford one more. We add up their existing EMIs and compare them with their income. If they have made many enquiries in a short time, it may mean other lenders have turned them down, or that they are in money trouble.

The bureau also helps us set the loan terms. A customer with a long, clean history may get a better rate or a higher amount. A customer with a short or patchy history may get a smaller first loan. This is fair to both sides.

We also use bureau data to catch fraud. If the name, date of birth, address or phone number on the application does not match the bureau record, that is a warning sign. Some fraud rings use real people's identities. Bureau checks help us find this.

After the loan is given, we keep using bureau data. Every month or quarter, we pull fresh data on our existing customers. This shows us if they have taken new loans elsewhere or started missing payments to other lenders. Often, a customer stops paying other lenders before they stop paying us. This gives us an early warning, and our collection team can reach out before the problem grows.

Bureau data has some limits. Many people in India, especially in small towns and villages, have never taken a formal loan. They have no bureau record, so the bureau cannot tell us anything about them. We call them new to credit. For them, we use other information such as bank statements, income checks, and visits to their home or business. The bureau data can also have errors. A customer may be shown as a defaulter on a loan they have already paid. When customers point this out, we help them raise a dispute with the lender and the bureau.

There is also a duty on us as a lender. We must report correct data on time. Wrong reporting can hurt a customer's ability to get a loan for years. RBI rules now also require lenders to inform customers when their data is reported as a default and to fix errors within set timelines. If we do not, we can be made to pay compensation.

In short, bureau data is one of the most useful tools we have. But it works best when used with good judgement and other information, not as the only basis for a decision.

prompt: How do you manage personal stress and decision fatigue as a senior leader?
text:
Not always well, if I'm honest. There was a stretch in 2020 when I was on calls from 7 in the morning till past 11 at night, and by about week six I noticed I was snapping at people over things that didn't matter. My wife pointed it out before I did.

A few things help. I try to make the big calls in the morning, when I'm fresh, and I push routine approvals into a fixed slot after lunch so they don't eat my whole day. I walk most evenings, phone in pocket, no podcasts. I've got two or three people outside work, old friends mainly, who don't care what my title is, and talking to them resets things. Sleep's non-negotiable now too, which it definitely wasn't in my thirties.

And I've learned to delegate decisions properly, not just tasks. If I've hired good people, I don't need to be in every loop. That's been the hardest habit to break, but it's made the biggest difference.

prompt: How should lenders approach recovery under the SARFAESI Act?
text:
The SARFAESI Act, 2002 is a very powerful tool for secured lenders, since it allows enforcement of security interest without the intervention of the court. NBFCs with an asset size of Rs 100 crore and above are eligible to use the same for secured loans of Rs 20 lakh and above, as per the notification of February 2021. For HFCs and NBFCs doing LAP and home loans, it is therefore an important part of the recovery toolkit.

The process is well defined. Once the account is classified as NPA, the lender issues a demand notice under Section 13(2), giving the borrower 60 days to repay. If the borrower fails to do so, the lender may take symbolic possession under Section 13(4), and thereafter approach the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate under Section 14 for physical possession, before proceeding for auction.

However, I would like to emphasise that SARFAESI should be used judiciously and not as a first step. In my experience, the notice itself brings a good number of borrowers to the table for settlement. Lenders should ensure that all procedural requirements are strictly followed, since any lapse in the notice, valuation or auction process gives the borrower ground to approach the DRT and can delay recovery by years. Proper documentation at the time of sanction itself, including clean title and a correctly registered mortgage with CERSAI, makes all the difference at the time of enforcement.

prompt: How should an NBFC manage liquidity risk?
text:
Liquidity risk is arguably the most dangerous risk an NBFC faces, because it can bring down an otherwise solvent institution within weeks. Unlike banks, NBFCs do not have access to low-cost retail deposits (except for a limited number of deposit-taking entities) or to the RBI's liquidity windows in the normal course, so they depend on wholesale funding from banks, mutual funds, insurance companies and bond investors. When confidence in the sector weakens, as it did after the IL&FS default in 2018, that funding can dry up quickly.

Managing liquidity risk well starts with a clear understanding of the institution's cash flow profile. The ALCO should regularly review the structural liquidity statement across time buckets, paying particular attention to cumulative mismatches in the near-term buckets, and should monitor dynamic liquidity projections that incorporate expected disbursements, collections and debt servicing over the next three to six months.

Second, the funding mix should be diversified. Over-reliance on any single source, especially short-term commercial paper used to fund long-term loans, creates fragility. A healthy profile typically blends bank term loans, NCDs of varying tenors, securitisation and direct assignment, refinance from institutions such as NHB or SIDBI where eligible, and possibly external commercial borrowings.

Third, the NBFC should hold an adequate liquidity buffer. Larger NBFCs are required to maintain a liquidity coverage ratio, holding high-quality liquid assets sufficient to cover stressed net outflows over 30 days. Beyond the regulatory minimum, many well-run NBFCs keep enough liquidity, including undrawn committed bank lines, to cover several months of debt repayments without any fresh borrowing.

Fourth, stress testing should be taken seriously. Scenarios should include a freeze in capital market funding, a sharp slowdown in collections and a rating downgrade, with the board reviewing how long the institution could survive under each.

Fifth, there should be a contingency funding plan with clear triggers, responsibilities and actions, such as pausing disbursements, drawing on committed lines or selling liquid assets, so that the response in a crisis is fast and coordinated.

Liquidity buffers carry a cost in the form of negative carry, and there is always pressure to minimise them in good times. Resisting that pressure is one of the most important responsibilities of an NBFC's leadership.

prompt: How would you use the Balanced Scorecard for a lending business?
text:
The Balanced Scorecard, developed by Robert Kaplan and David Norton, offers a structured means of translating an organisation's strategy into a coherent set of performance measures across four perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth. For a lending business, the framework is particularly valuable because it counteracts the natural tendency to focus disproportionately on disbursement volumes and short-term profitability at the expense of the underlying drivers of sustainable performance.

The financial perspective should capture both growth and the quality of that growth. Appropriate measures include growth in assets under management, net interest margin, credit cost as a percentage of average assets, the cost-to-income ratio, return on assets and return on equity. Gross and net non-performing asset ratios should be included here or, alternatively, under a separate risk dimension, which some lenders add as a fifth perspective given the centrality of credit risk to the business model.

The customer perspective should reflect the institution's value proposition to its target segments. For a retail lender operating in Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets, relevant measures may include turnaround time from application to disbursement, net promoter score, complaint incidence per ten thousand accounts, complaints escalated to the Ombudsman, retention rates on balance transfer requests, and the share of new-to-credit customers served.

The internal process perspective should address the operational capabilities that underpin the customer proposition and financial results. Measures may include first-time-right rates for loan files, the proportion of applications processed digitally, early delinquency rates by sourcing channel, collection efficiency in each bucket, fraud detection rates and audit observations. These metrics allow management to identify process deficiencies before they manifest in financial outcomes.

The learning and growth perspective concerns the people, systems and culture on which the organisation depends. In lending, this would typically include attrition among frontline sales and collections staff, training hours per employee, internal promotion rates, the proportion of critical roles with identified successors, and progress on technology initiatives such as loan origination system upgrades.

The value of the Balanced Scorecard lies not merely in the selection of measures but in the explicit causal linkages between them. For instance, reduced attrition among credit officers is expected to improve underwriting consistency, which in turn should lower early delinquency and credit costs, ultimately improving return on equity. Articulating these linkages in a strategy map enables leadership to test its assumptions and to explain to employees how their work contributes to institutional objectives.

In implementation, the scorecard should be cascaded from the enterprise level to business units, regions and branches, with targets calibrated to local conditions. It should be reviewed at least quarterly by senior management and periodically by the board. Care should be taken to limit the number of measures, typically to between fifteen and twenty-five at the enterprise level, so that the scorecard remains a tool for focus rather than an exhaustive catalogue of statistics.

prompt: What lessons did the IL&FS crisis teach NBFCs about liquidity?
text:
I was the CFO of a housing finance company with an AUM of around ₹11,000 crore when IL&FS defaulted in September 2018, so the lessons for me are not theoretical. They were learned in a very uncomfortable few months.

At the time, about 22% of our borrowings were commercial paper, most of it with tenors of 90 days or less, and almost all of it placed with mutual funds.
