On paper, our ALM looked acceptable because we were assuming rollovers. In the last week of September, two large fund houses told us they would not roll over ₹600 crore of CP maturing in October. Within three weeks, our CP spreads had gone from about 30 basis points over T-bills to over 150 basis points, and some funds were simply not taking calls. We had roughly ₹2,100 crore of maturities in the following 90 days.

We got through it, but only because of three things. We had about ₹900 crore of undrawn sanctioned bank lines that we drew down immediately. We did two direct assignment transactions with public sector banks totalling about ₹1,400 crore at short notice, which was possible only because our home loan book was clean and well documented. And we slowed disbursements from about ₹450 crore a month to under ₹150 crore for nearly two quarters. That last step hurt our business and our DSA relationships badly, but it was necessary.

The first lesson I took away is that rollover risk is real risk, and a funding source that can disappear in a week should never fund assets that run for fifteen years. After the crisis, we brought CP down to under 5% of borrowings and capped it at the level of our liquid investments plus undrawn lines. Our weighted average cost of funds went up by about 35 basis points, and I had to defend that to the board more than once. I would do it again.

The second lesson is that a liquidity buffer is only useful if it is truly available. Some of the instruments we had counted as liquid turned out to be hard to sell at a fair price in a panic. Today I count only government securities, treasury bills, bank fixed deposits and committed undrawn lines in my buffer, and I size it to cover at least three months of debt servicing with no new borrowing.

The third lesson is about the quality of the asset book. The reason we could sell portfolios at short notice was that buyers trusted our underwriting. Peers with weaker books, or with large wholesale exposures to real estate developers, found no buyers at any reasonable price. Asset quality and liquidity are not separate topics.

The fourth lesson is about communication. In October 2018, I spent more time talking to banks, mutual funds and rating agencies than to my own team. We started sharing a monthly liquidity update with our top 15 lenders, voluntarily, and we have continued doing it. Transparency builds the kind of trust that keeps funding lines open when the market turns.

Finally, the crisis showed that the regulatory framework had gaps. The RBI's subsequent introduction of the liquidity coverage ratio for NBFCs and stricter ALM guidelines were the right response. But regulation sets the floor. Each board has to decide for itself how much liquidity insurance it is willing to pay for in good times.

prompt: What is your view on the Account Aggregator framework?
text:
The Account Aggregator framework is one of the most useful changes in Indian finance in recent years. I think it will matter a lot for lenders, especially those who serve small businesses and people without a long credit history. But it also has limits, and it will take time to reach its full use.

First, what is it? An Account Aggregator, or AA, is a company licensed by the RBI to move financial data from one institution to another, with the customer's consent. The AA itself cannot read or store the data. It only passes it along, in encrypted form. The institution that holds the data, such as a bank, is called a Financial Information Provider. The institution that wants the data, such as a lender, is called a Financial Information User. The customer approves each request through an app. The approval says what data is shared, for what purpose, and for how long. The customer can cancel it at any time.

Why does this matter for lending? Before AA, if a lender wanted to see a customer's bank statements, the customer had to download PDFs and upload them, or share their net banking password with a third-party tool. Both methods had problems. PDFs could be edited. Sharing passwords was unsafe. Many customers found the whole thing confusing and dropped out of the application.

With AA, the data comes straight from the bank in a standard format. It cannot be faked. It arrives in seconds. The customer does not have to share any password. This makes the process faster, safer and more reliable for both sides.

For lenders, the biggest benefit is better decisions for people with thin credit files. A small shop owner may have no loan history, but his bank account shows money coming in every day. A young salaried person may not have a credit card, but her salary credits show a stable job. With AA, lenders can see this quickly and use it to judge the risk. Over time, as more types of data come into the system, such as GST, insurance, mutual funds and pension records, the picture will become richer.

AA also helps after the loan is given. With the customer's consent, a lender can look at the bank account from time to time and spot early signs of stress, such as falling balances or bounced payments. This allows the lender to act early.

There are some challenges. First, not all banks share data equally well. Some have slow or unreliable systems, and the success rate of data requests varies. Second, many customers still do not understand what they are agreeing to. The consent screen needs to be simple and in local languages. Third, lenders must use the data responsibly. They should take only what they need and use it only for the stated purpose. If lenders misuse this data, people will stop trusting the system. Fourth, AA works best for customers who use formal bank accounts heavily. A borrower who deals mostly in cash will still need traditional checks.

I also think the industry needs to get better at using the data, not just collecting it. Pulling twelve months of bank statements is easy. Turning them into a sound credit view takes good analytics and experienced credit staff.

Overall, my view is positive. The AA framework is a well-designed piece of public digital infrastructure, in the same family as UPI and Aadhaar-based e-KYC. It puts the customer in control of their own data, which is the right principle. For lenders willing to invest in using it properly, it can lower costs, cut fraud and bring many more people into formal credit. I expect that within a few years, consent-based data sharing will be a normal part of almost every loan application in India.

prompt: What's your view on BNPL and small-ticket personal loans?
text:
Mixed, honestly. I get the appeal. First job, no credit history, and someone needs ₹8,000 for a phone or a course fee. Small-ticket credit can be a genuinely useful on-ramp, and a few people I know built their first bureau record that way.

But I've also seen what happens when it's done badly. A colleague's nephew had five of these apps on his phone at one point. None of the loans was big on its own. Together, with the fees and the late charges, he was paying something like 60% a year and borrowing from one app to pay the other. He didn't even think of it as debt. It was just 'pay later.'

That's the core problem. The product's designed to feel frictionless, and friction is sometimes the thing that stops people overborrowing.

RBI's digital lending rules have cleaned up a lot, which is good. Disclosure, direct disbursal, no more murky pass-through arrangements. But as a lender, I'd still want sensible limits, real affordability checks and honest pricing before I put my balance sheet behind it. Small ticket doesn't mean small risk.

prompt: What is your view on partnerships with real estate builders for home loan sourcing?
text:
Builder tie-ups, also known as Approved Project Finance (APF) arrangements, have been an important source of home loan business for banks and HFCs in India. Under such arrangements, the lender carries out legal and technical due diligence of the project upfront, and thereafter the buyers in the project can avail home loans with much faster processing. For the lender, it gives access to a ready pool of customers at a lower acquisition cost, and for the builder it helps in faster sales.

In my view, these partnerships are useful but they need to be handled very carefully. The 2017-2020 period has given us several painful lessons in this regard. Many projects in NCR and other markets got stalled, and home buyers who had availed loans under subvention schemes were left paying EMIs on flats which were never delivered. In some cases, lenders had disbursed far ahead of construction progress, on the basis of builder demand only.

Hence, a few safeguards are necessary. Firstly, the lender must assess the builder's track record, financial position and RERA compliance before approving the project. Secondly, disbursement must be strictly linked to the stage of construction, as certified by an independent technical valuer, and not to the builder's payment schedule. Thirdly, subvention or pre-EMI schemes where the builder pays the interest on behalf of the buyer should be avoided or kept to a minimum, since these create hidden risk. Fourthly, concentration limits per builder and per project must be laid down in the credit policy itself.

Done properly, builder partnerships remain a good channel, especially in Tier 2 cities where organised developers are growing. But the lender must never forget that the borrower is the home buyer and the security is the flat, so the quality of the project matters as much as the quality of the customer.

prompt: How do you approach provisioning under the Ind AS 109 expected credit loss framework?
text:
Under Ind AS 109, NBFCs that have transitioned to Ind AS recognise loan loss provisions on an expected credit loss basis rather than the incurred loss approach that underpins the RBI's income recognition and asset classification norms. The ECL approach requires a lender to estimate losses expected to arise over a defined horizon, taking into account forward-looking information, which makes it both more responsive to changing conditions and more dependent on judgement.

The framework classifies loans into three stages. Stage 1 covers performing accounts without a significant increase in credit risk, typically those up to 30 days past due, and attracts a 12-month ECL. Stage 2 includes accounts where credit risk has increased significantly since origination, commonly those between 31 and 90 days past due or those meeting other qualitative triggers such as restructuring, and attracts a lifetime ECL. Stage 3 comprises credit-impaired accounts, generally those more than 90 days past due, also with lifetime ECL.

My approach to building a robust ECL framework would rest on a few principles. First, segment the portfolio meaningfully. Home loans, LAP, vehicle loans and unsecured loans behave very differently, and within each product, factors such as customer type, geography and ticket size can matter. Probability of default, loss given default and exposure at default should be estimated at a granularity that reflects these differences without becoming statistically unreliable.

Second, use forward-looking macroeconomic information sensibly. ECL models typically incorporate scenarios for variables such as GDP growth, inflation or sector-specific indicators, weighted by probability. These links should be economically intuitive and periodically back-tested, rather than introduced mechanically.

Third, define the significant increase in credit risk criteria thoughtfully. Relying only on the 30 days past due backstop can be too late. Bureau deterioration, restructuring or early warning signals can serve as useful additional triggers.

Fourth, apply management overlays with discipline. During events like the COVID-19 pandemic, historical data clearly did not capture the risk, and overlays were appropriate. However, overlays should be documented, quantified with a clear rationale, reviewed by the audit committee, and released only when the underlying risk has actually reduced, not to smooth earnings.

Finally, reconcile with regulatory requirements. The RBI requires NBFCs on Ind AS to compare ECL provisions with those required under IRACP norms and to maintain an impairment reserve where ECL is lower. Strong governance across risk, finance and the audit committee, together with independent model validation, is what gives auditors, investors and the regulator confidence in the numbers.

prompt: How should NBFCs approach IT governance and cybersecurity?
text:
The increasing digitisation of lending operations has fundamentally altered the risk profile of non-banking financial companies. Loan origination, underwriting, disbursement, collections and customer servicing are now heavily dependent on technology platforms, many of which are integrated with external partners such as lending service providers, payment aggregators, credit bureaus and Account Aggregators. In this environment, information technology governance and cybersecurity are no longer technical concerns to be delegated entirely to the IT function; they are matters of enterprise risk requiring the attention of the board and senior management.

The Reserve Bank of India has recognised this through its Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices, issued in November 2023 and applicable from April 2024 to NBFCs in the upper and middle layers, among other regulated entities. The direction requires regulated entities to establish a board-level IT Strategy Committee, an IT Steering Committee at the management level, and an information security function headed by a Chief Information Security Officer who is independent of IT operations. It further addresses business continuity, disaster recovery, vendor risk management and the conduct of periodic information systems audits.

Compliance with these requirements constitutes the minimum standard. An effective approach should, in addition, be grounded in the following principles.

First, the board should articulate a clear risk appetite for technology and cyber risk, including tolerances for system downtime, data loss and third-party exposure. This appetite should inform investment decisions and should be reviewed in light of evolving threats.

Second, the institution should maintain a comprehensive inventory of its information assets, applications and data flows, including those managed by third parties. Customer data, in particular, should be classified by sensitivity and protected accordingly, consistent with the requirements of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Third, third-party risk deserves particular emphasis. Lending partnerships frequently involve the sharing of customer data with fintech partners and service providers whose security standards may be uneven. Due diligence prior to onboarding, contractual provisions on data protection and audit rights, and periodic assessments are essential.

Fourth, the institution should invest in detection and response capabilities, not merely prevention. A security operations centre, whether internal or outsourced, should monitor systems continuously, and incident response plans should be tested through simulated exercises. Reportable incidents must be notified to the Reserve Bank of India and CERT-In within the prescribed timelines.

Fifth, human factors should not be underestimated. A significant proportion of breaches originate from phishing, weak credentials or inadvertent errors by employees. Regular training, simulated phishing exercises and strict access controls based on the principle of least privilege are effective mitigants.

Finally, the board and senior management should receive regular, intelligible reporting on cyber risk, including key risk indicators, the status of audit observations and the results of penetration testing. Directors need not be technical specialists, but they must be sufficiently informed to challenge management and to satisfy themselves that the institution's defences are commensurate with the risks it faces.

prompt: How do you lead change management during a core system migration?
text:
In FY2021-22, I led the migration of our entire loan book, about 3,40,000 accounts and ₹16,800 crore of AUM, from a fifteen-year-old legacy loan management system to a new cloud-based core platform. It took nineteen months instead of the twelve we had planned, cost about ₹68 crore against a budget of ₹52 crore, and the three weeks after go-live were the most stressful period of my career. But it worked, and I learned more about change management from that project than from any course.

The first thing I would say is that a core system migration is not an IT project. I made that mistake at the start. We set it up with the CIO as the project owner and business heads as stakeholders. Within four months, it was clear that nobody in the business felt it was theirs. Requirements were being signed off by junior people who did not understand the downstream effects. We reset the governance so that I chaired a fortnightly steering committee, each business head owned the sign-off for their product's migration, and the CIO's role was to deliver, not to decide.

Second, you have to be honest about what people are losing. Our branch operations staff had used the old system for years. They knew every workaround. The new system was better in almost every way, but it was unfamiliar, and for many of them it felt like their expertise had suddenly become worthless. We identified about 120 champions across branches, mostly experienced operations officers, and gave them early access, extra training and a role in testing. They became the people others turned to, and their credibility was far greater than anything head office could say.

Third, data migration is where projects fail. We ran four full mock migrations before go-live. In the first one, about 11% of accounts had reconciliation differences in outstanding balance, interest accrual or charges. By the fourth, it was under 0.3%, and each of those was explained. I insisted that finance and internal audit sign off on reconciliation independently. It added about six weeks to the timeline, and I am glad we did it.

Fourth, plan for the bad days after go-live. We went live over a long weekend in November 2021. On the first Monday, NACH presentation files did not generate correctly for about 18,000 accounts, and we had to re-present manually. Customer calls to our contact centre went up threefold for two weeks. We had prepared for this with a war room staffed round the clock, pre-drafted customer communication and a clear escalation matrix, so we managed it, but it was not pretty. I would advise anyone in this position to tell the board in advance that there will be problems in the first month, so that when they come, they do not look like failure.

Fifth, communicate more than you think is necessary. I sent a short weekly note to all employees for the last six months of the project, explaining what was happening, what was going well and what was not. I also held open-house video calls where anyone could ask questions. People handle change much better when they do not feel it is being done to them in secret.

Finally, measure the benefits honestly afterwards. Within a year, our month-end closing time came down from nine days to four, the number of staff on manual reconciliation reduced by about 40%, and we were able to launch two new products in weeks rather than months. Sharing those results with the teams who had suffered through the transition mattered. It gave the whole exercise a sense of purpose, and it made the next change easier.

prompt: How would you approach gold loan business strategy?
text:
Gold loans are simple to explain and quick to give. The customer brings gold. We check its purity and weight. We lend a part of its value, and the customer gets the money in under an hour. That speed is the main reason people choose us.

My strategy would rest on a few things. First, location. Gold loan branches need to be close to customers, in small towns and busy markets. Second, trust. Customers must feel their gold is safe, so storage and insurance must be strong. Third, fair valuation. Staff must test gold properly and follow RBI's limits on loan-to-value. Fourth, fraud control. Fake gold and staff theft are real risks, so we need regular audits and surprise checks. Gold prices also move, so we must watch the value of the gold we hold and act early if prices fall sharply.

I would also price fairly and make it easy to renew or close the loan. Most gold loan customers come back again and again, so treating them well pays off.

prompt: How do you approach diversity and inclusion in a lending organisation, especially women in field roles?
text:
I'll be honest, we were pretty bad at this for a long time. In 2018, women were maybe 4% of our field sales and collections staff. The excuse was always the same: it's a tough job, lots of travel on two-wheelers, late evenings, rural areas. Nobody ever really tested whether that was true.

What changed things for us was a branch manager in Coimbatore who just went ahead and hired three women as relationship officers, mostly to meet a hiring target. Within a year, two of them were among the best performers in the region. Their customers, a lot of them women running small businesses, actually preferred dealing with them. Collections were cleaner too.

So we started being deliberate about it. We fixed obvious stuff first, like safe travel reimbursement, no field visits after 7 p.m. unless someone chose to, and proper toilets in branches (which sounds basic, and it is, and several branches didn't have them). We set a hiring target per region rather than a quota on individual managers. And we paid attention to who was dropping out and why, because hiring women is the easy part and keeping them is harder.

We're at about 17% now in field roles. Not great, but it's a different company. And frankly, it's made us better at serving women borrowers, who are a big and underserved market. It wasn't charity. It was good business we'd been ignoring.

prompt: How would you respond to an adverse finding in an RBI inspection?
text:
An adverse finding in the RBI's inspection or supervisory review must be taken very seriously, since the same reflects on the governance and compliance culture of the institution. At the same time, it should not be seen only as a negative event. In my experience, the inspection team often points out issues which the management itself had overlooked or underestimated, and hence it is an opportunity to strengthen the systems.

The first step is to understand the observation in full. The Risk Assessment Report and the Risk Mitigation Plan shared by the RBI should be studied in detail by the senior management, compliance and the concerned business and risk heads. Wherever there is a genuine difference of opinion on facts, the same should be represented to the RBI with proper documentation, in a respectful manner and within the stipulated timeline. However, we should avoid being defensive merely for the sake of it.

Secondly, the root cause must be identified. For instance, if the finding pertains to deviations in KYC or delays in NPA classification, we need to find out whether it is a system issue, a process gap, a training gap or a case of wilful non-compliance by some officials. Only then can the corrective action be effective.

Thirdly, a time-bound action plan with clear ownership has to be prepared and placed before the Audit Committee and the Board. Progress on each item should be tracked monthly, and the compliance status should be submitted to the RBI as required. Where systems changes are needed, the IT team should be involved from day one itself.

Fourthly, accountability must be fixed wherever there are lapses. This sends a clear message across the organisation.

Lastly, the management should check whether the same issue exists in other products or regions which were not part of the sample. Kindly remember that a repeat observation in the next inspection is viewed very adversely by the regulator and may invite monetary penalty or business restrictions. Hence, closure must be in letter and spirit both.

prompt: What are the strategic implications of RBI's November 2023 increase in risk weights on unsecured consumer credit?
text:
In November 2023, the RBI raised the risk weights on consumer credit exposures of banks and NBFCs, including personal loans, from 100% to 125%, and increased risk weights on credit card receivables. It also raised the risk weights on bank lending to NBFCs by 25 percentage points where the existing risk weight, based on the NBFC's rating, was below 100%. Housing loans, education loans, vehicle loans, loans against gold and microfinance loans were excluded. The move was a clear signal that the regulator was uncomfortable with the pace of growth in unsecured retail credit and with the interconnectedness between banks and the NBFCs that funded such growth.

The strategic implications for NBFCs operate on several levels.

The most direct effect was on capital. A higher risk weight means more capital is needed for the same book, which reduces return on equity unless pricing increases. For NBFCs with large unsecured personal loan portfolios, this forced a reassessment of how much of their growth plan was still economically attractive, and several moderated growth targets or raised capital.

The second effect was on funding costs. Because banks now needed more capital against their loans to many NBFCs, they passed on part of that cost through higher lending rates. NBFCs rated in the AA and A categories, which depend heavily on bank borrowing, felt this most. This accelerated efforts to diversify funding through bonds, securitisation, co-lending and, for larger players, external commercial borrowings.

Third, the change shifted the relative attractiveness of products. Secured segments that were exempt, such as home loans, gold loans and vehicle finance, became comparatively more attractive from a capital perspective. Many diversified NBFCs rebalanced their product mix accordingly, and the gold loan segment in particular saw intensified competition.

Fourth, the move highlighted regulatory risk as a strategic variable in its own right. The RBI followed it with closer supervisory attention on unsecured lending, digital lending partnerships and small-ticket loans. NBFCs that had built their strategy around fast growth in small, unsecured, digitally sourced loans had to reassess underwriting standards, partner arrangements and collections capacity, particularly as delinquencies in some of these segments rose during 2024.

Fifth, it reinforced the importance of differentiation. A blanket risk weight does not distinguish between a carefully underwritten personal loan to a salaried customer with a strong bureau history and a high-risk loan sourced through an aggressive channel. Lenders whose portfolios genuinely performed better could still earn adequate returns, while those competing mainly on volume and price found their economics under pressure.

In the longer term, the episode encourages NBFCs to build balanced portfolios, stronger capital buffers and more diversified funding, and to treat the regulator's views on systemic risk as an early indicator of where the cycle may be heading. The RBI's decision in early 2025 to roll back the additional risk weight on bank lending to NBFCs also underlines that the regulatory environment is itself dynamic, and that strategy needs to remain flexible enough to respond in either direction.

prompt: How should an NBFC diversify its borrowing profile?
text:
The composition of an NBFC's liabilities is as important to its long-term viability as the quality of its assets. Unlike banks, most NBFCs do not have access to retail deposits and must rely on wholesale funding, which is inherently more sensitive to market sentiment, credit ratings and regulatory developments. Concentration in any single source or instrument therefore exposes the institution to the risk that funding becomes unavailable or prohibitively expensive at precisely the moment it is most needed. A deliberate strategy for diversifying the borrowing profile should accordingly be a standing priority for the board and senior management.

Diversification should be pursued along four dimensions: lender type, instrument, tenor and geography.

With respect to lender type, NBFCs have historically depended heavily on bank borrowings, which in many cases account for more than half of total liabilities. While bank funding provides stability and relationship continuity, excessive dependence makes the institution vulnerable to changes in bank risk appetite and regulatory treatment, as demonstrated by the increase in risk weights on bank exposures to NBFCs in November 2023. Mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds, development finance institutions and, for eligible entities, refinance institutions such as the National Housing Bank, SIDBI and NABARD offer complementary sources.

With respect to instruments, the institution should maintain access to a range of products, including term loans, non-convertible debentures, commercial paper within prudent limits, subordinated debt, securitisation and direct assignment transactions, and co-lending arrangements. Securitisation and direct assignment are particularly valuable, since they transfer assets off the balance sheet, provide funding at rates that reflect the quality of the underlying pool rather than the rating of the originator, and remain available even when unsecured borrowing becomes difficult. Public issuance of NCDs to retail investors can further broaden the investor base, although it entails additional disclosure and operational obligations.

With respect to tenor, the borrowing profile should be aligned as closely as practicable with the maturity profile of assets. Excessive reliance on short-term instruments to fund long-term loans was a principal cause of the distress experienced by several NBFCs following the IL&FS default in 2018. A laddered maturity profile, which avoids the concentration of repayments in any single month or quarter, reduces refinancing risk.

With respect to geography, larger NBFCs with adequate ratings may access external commercial borrowings and multilateral funding. These sources can extend tenor and broaden the investor base, although the associated currency risk must be hedged in accordance with the regulatory framework, and the all-in cost should be evaluated carefully against domestic alternatives.

Diversification does not occur by default; it requires sustained investment. Investor relationships must be developed over time, including during periods when the funding is not immediately required. Transparent and consistent disclosure, a strong credit rating, demonstrable asset quality and sound governance are prerequisites for access to the broadest range of investors. The treasury function should be adequately staffed and empowered to cultivate these relationships.

Finally, the board should establish explicit concentration limits, for example on the share of borrowings from the largest lenders, on the proportion of short-term funding and on the share of any single instrument, and should monitor compliance through the Asset Liability Committee. Some additional cost is inevitable in maintaining a diversified profile, but this cost should be viewed as insurance against a far more damaging loss of access to funding.

prompt: What factors would you consider before expanding branches into Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns?
text:
Between FY2019-20 and FY2023-24, we grew from 118 to 286 branches, almost all of the new ones in Tier 2, Tier 3 and smaller towns across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Maharashtra. About 70% of those branches are doing well today. Around 15% are average, and the remaining 15% or so we either merged or would not open again if we had the choice. Most of what I would advise on this question comes from understanding why those last two groups did not work.

The first factor is the depth of the local economy, and I mean depth rather than size. A town with a population of two lakh but a single dominant industry is far riskier than a town of one lakh with a mix of agriculture, trading, small manufacturing and government employment. We opened two branches in a textile cluster that looked very attractive on the numbers. When that industry went through a downturn in 2022, almost the entire branch portfolio came under stress at once. Now we look at the composition of local income sources, the number of GST-registered businesses, bank deposit growth in the district and property registration data before we decide.

The second factor is competition and pricing. If five banks and four NBFCs are already present, the good customers have choices, and we will end up with the ones others rejected unless we have a real edge. In some towns, it made more sense to enter through a hub-and-spoke model, with a small satellite office and periodic visits from a larger branch nearby, rather than a full branch.

The third factor is people. In my experience, the single biggest predictor of a new branch's success is the branch manager. Someone from the region, who speaks the language and understands local property titles, informal income patterns and social dynamics, is far more valuable than a high performer transplanted from a metro. Of our weakest branches, more than half had a branch manager who was not from the region and who left within eighteen months.

The fourth factor is legal and collateral infrastructure. Property-backed lending depends on reliable title records, the availability of good local lawyers and valuers and, eventually, the ability to enforce security. In some districts, land records were digitised and clean. In others, title verification took weeks and carried real risk. We now include a legal and technical feasibility review before approving any new location.

The fifth factor is unit economics. A typical new branch for us costs about ₹35 to ₹40 lakh to set up and around ₹8 lakh a month to run, including staff. With our average ticket size of about ₹12 lakh and our yields on LAP and affordable home loans, a branch needs a book of roughly ₹40 crore to break even, which typically takes 24 to 30 months. We now model every proposed location against this and are honest about the assumptions.

The sixth factor is sequencing. We learned that it is better to cluster branches within a region than to scatter them. A cluster of eight to ten branches within a few hours of each other can share a regional credit manager, a legal panel, a collections team and a trainer. Isolated branches far from any support struggled with supervision and quality.

Finally, I would consider the company's own readiness. Expansion stretches every function: credit, operations, HR, audit and IT. In FY2021-22, we opened 52 branches in one year, and our internal audit and training teams simply could not keep up. Early delinquencies in that cohort were noticeably higher. Since then, we have capped openings at around 35 a year.

In summary, Tier 2 and Tier 3 expansion can be very rewarding, and our yields and customer loyalty in these markets are better than in the metros. But it rewards patience, local knowledge and careful selection far more than speed.

prompt: How do you balance growth and profitability?
text:
Growth and profit can pull in different directions. If we grow too fast, we may lend to weaker borrowers, spend too much on new branches, or cut prices to win business. Profit falls later. If we focus only on profit, we may stop investing and lose ground to others.

I try to balance the two in a few simple ways.

First, I look at returns, not just size. A product that grows fast but earns less than our cost of capital is not worth growing. I want to know the return on equity for each product after credit losses and costs.

Second, I look at how loans perform over time. A loan book can look healthy in its first year and go bad in its third. So I judge growth by how the loans perform, not by how many we give.

Third, I invest in growth in steps. New branches and new products get a fixed budget and a clear target. If they do not meet it, we stop or change course.

Fourth, I keep costs under control as we grow. Each new rupee of loans should cost less to service than the last.

The goal is growth that pays for itself over time.

prompt: How should traditional NBFCs respond to competition from fintechs?
text:
I remember around 2019 there was a lot of panic in our industry about fintechs. Every conference had a panel called something like 'Will fintechs eat the NBFC's lunch?' Our board asked me about it at least twice. And to be fair, some of those companies were impressive. Ten-minute approvals, slick apps, no branch visits.

Six or seven years on, the picture's more nuanced. A lot of the fintechs that tried to lend off their own balance sheets found out that underwriting and collections are hard, and that cheap customer acquisition through an app doesn't mean much if a chunk of those customers don't pay you back. Many of them ended up partnering with banks and NBFCs, or getting an NBFC licence themselves and slowly looking more like us.

So I don't think the right response is to panic or to try to become a fintech overnight. It's to be honest about where they're better than you and fix that. For us it was mostly speed and convenience. Our home loan customers didn't care about a fancy app, but they really cared about not having to come to the branch four times and submit the same documents twice. Fixing that took us about eighteen months and didn't need anything revolutionary. Just digitising the journey properly.

Where we've got an edge, we've doubled down. Knowing self-employed customers in small towns, being able to assess a property title in Bhilwara, having someone who'll sit with the customer when there's a problem. That's hard to build from Bengaluru.

And partnering has actually worked better than competing in a few cases. We've got two co-lending and sourcing tie-ups with fintechs now, and both sides bring something the other doesn't have.

prompt: How do you think about loan against property (LAP) as a product?
text:
Loan Against Property is one of the core products for NBFCs and HFCs in India, especially for the self-employed segment. Basically, the customer mortgages his residential or commercial property and avails a loan for business purposes, for working capital, for children's education or marriage, or for consolidation of high-cost debt. Ticket sizes may range from ₹5 lakh in smaller towns to several crores in metro markets.

The product has several attractive features from the lender's point of view. Firstly, it is secured by immovable property, which the borrower is generally very reluctant to lose, and hence repayment discipline is reasonably good. Secondly, yields are higher than home loans, typically in the range of 11% to 16% depending upon the segment, while credit costs are moderate if underwriting is done properly. Thirdly, tenures are long, which gives good AUM stability.

However, LAP is not a risk-free product, and lenders who treated it as such have suffered. I would like to highlight a few points in this regard.

The end use of LAP is not always easy to monitor. Funds which are meant for business purposes may get diverted to speculative activities or to repay other loans. Hence, cash flow assessment of the borrower's business is critical. The property is only a secondary source of repayment and should not be the primary basis for the credit decision.

Valuation risk is another important concern. Property in smaller towns is not very liquid, and in case of default, the realisable value may be much lower than what the valuation report says. Therefore, LTV should be kept conservative, generally in the range of 50% to 60%, and valuation must be done by empanelled valuers with periodic sampling and re-verification.

Title and legal risk also needs to be carefully examined, especially in case of ancestral property, property in rural areas or where there are multiple owners. A proper title search going back 13 to 30 years, along with correct registration of the mortgage, is a must.

Lastly, the LAP market has become very competitive, with banks offering lower rates to the better customers. NBFCs should therefore focus on the segments where they have a genuine advantage, i.e. small business owners with informal income in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns, rather than competing on rate only.

prompt: How would you manage a portfolio with a high share of restructured accounts?
text:
A portfolio with a large share of restructured accounts needs a distinct management approach, because restructured loans behave differently from both standard performing loans and outright NPAs. Many Indian lenders faced this situation after the COVID-19 Resolution Frameworks of 2020 and 2021, when significant portions of retail and MSME books were restructured, and the experience from that period offers useful guidance.

The first step is to understand the composition of the restructured book in detail. Restructuring is a blunt label covering very different situations. Some borrowers experienced a temporary disruption, such as a business closure during lockdown, and have since recovered. Others had pre-existing weaknesses that the pandemic exposed, and restructuring merely postponed an inevitable default. Segmenting the book by pre-restructuring payment history, the nature of the borrower's income, the type of relief granted, collateral cover and current repayment behaviour gives a much clearer picture of where the risk lies.

The second step is to monitor performance closely after the moratorium or relief period ends. The critical test of a restructured account is whether it resumes regular payments once the revised schedule begins. Tracking cohort-wise performance in the first six to twelve months after resumption is essential, since that is when most re-defaults occur. Under RBI norms, restructured accounts must also demonstrate satisfactory performance during a specified period before they can be upgraded, so monitoring is necessary for regulatory reasons too.

Third, provisioning should be realistic. Restructured accounts typically carry higher regulatory provisioning requirements, and under Ind AS 109 they would normally be classified at least in Stage 2, attracting lifetime expected credit loss. Lenders should resist the temptation to assume that all restructured borrowers will recover. Holding additional management overlays for the weakest segments is prudent until their performance is established.

Fourth, the collections strategy should be tailored. Borrowers who are paying regularly under the restructured terms should be supported with reminders and convenient payment channels, not treated as high-risk defaulters. Those who show early signs of re-default need prompt engagement to understand whether there is a genuine new problem or a lack of willingness to pay. For accounts that have clearly failed, the lender should move decisively to recovery through SARFAESI, settlement or sale to an asset reconstruction company rather than restructuring repeatedly, which usually only delays losses.

Fifth, communicate clearly with stakeholders. Investors, rating agencies and lenders will scrutinise the performance of the restructured book closely. Providing transparent data on its size, collection efficiency and re-default rates builds credibility, while vague disclosures tend to invite worst-case assumptions.

Finally, the experience should feed back into credit policy. Analysing which customer profiles needed restructuring and which subsequently recovered can improve underwriting for the next cycle. In many cases, lenders discovered that borrowers with diversified income sources, stronger bureau histories and lower leverage at origination were far more resilient, and adjusted their policies accordingly.

Handled carefully, a restructured portfolio can be worked down over two to three years with manageable losses. The main risk lies in either excessive optimism, which leads to under-provisioning, or excessive pessimism, which pushes borrowers who could have recovered into default.

prompt: How can a lending institution foster innovation while operating in a regulated environment?
text:
Innovation in a regulated financial institution is frequently perceived as a contradiction in terms. Regulation is designed to constrain risk-taking, ensure consistency and protect customers, while innovation by its nature involves experimentation, uncertainty and departure from established practice. In the experience of well-managed institutions, however, the two are not inherently in conflict. The regulatory framework defines the boundaries within which an institution must operate, but it leaves considerable scope for innovation in products, processes, distribution and customer experience. The challenge for leadership is to create an organisational environment in which such innovation can occur responsibly.

The first requirement is clarity of purpose. Innovation efforts should be directed at clearly articulated problems, such as reducing turnaround time for self-employed borrowers, lowering the cost of servicing small-ticket loans, improving collection outcomes in early buckets or extending credit to new-to-credit customers. Innovation pursued for its own sake, or in imitation of competitors, tends to consume resources without delivering commensurate value.

The second requirement is the early involvement of the risk and compliance functions. In many institutions, these functions are consulted only after a new initiative has been substantially developed, at which point their concerns are perceived as obstacles. A more effective model embeds risk and compliance professionals within innovation teams from the outset, so that regulatory requirements inform design choices rather than being imposed after the fact. Such involvement frequently identifies solutions that satisfy both business and regulatory objectives.

The third requirement is a structured approach to experimentation. Institutions should establish a framework for controlled pilots, with defined limits on exposure, duration, geography and customer numbers, clear success criteria and a governance mechanism for decisions on scaling or discontinuation. This allows new ideas to be tested with real customers while limiting potential losses. The Reserve Bank of India's regulatory sandbox provides an additional avenue for testing innovations that may require regulatory clarification.

The fourth requirement is a supportive culture. Employees must believe that thoughtful experimentation will be recognised and that failure, where it occurs within agreed parameters, will not be penalised. Senior leadership should communicate this explicitly and demonstrate it through its response to unsuccessful initiatives. At the same time, the institution must distinguish clearly between intelligent failure within a controlled experiment and carelessness or breaches of policy, which should continue to attract consequences.

The fifth requirement concerns partnerships. Many promising innovations in Indian lending have emerged from collaboration between regulated entities and technology companies, in areas such as alternative data analytics, digital onboarding, Account Aggregator integration and collections automation. Such partnerships can accelerate innovation considerably, but they must be governed with care. The regulated entity remains accountable for compliance with the digital lending directions, outsourcing guidelines, data protection obligations and fair practices requirements, irrespective of the role played by the partner.

The sixth requirement is appropriate investment in enabling infrastructure. Modern, modular technology platforms, clean and accessible data, and application programming interfaces that allow rapid integration with partners substantially reduce the cost and time required to test and launch new propositions. Institutions encumbered by legacy systems will find that even modest innovations require disproportionate effort.

Finally, the board has an important role to play. Directors should ensure that the institution's strategy includes explicit innovation objectives, that adequate resources are allocated, and that management reports periodically on progress. The board should also maintain a constructive dialogue with management on the institution's appetite for innovation-related risk, so that management has a clear mandate within which to act.

In summary, regulation need not stifle innovation. Institutions that combine a clear sense of purpose, early engagement with risk and compliance, disciplined experimentation and a supportive culture are well placed to innovate in ways that benefit customers and shareholders while preserving the confidence of the regulator.

prompt: Describe a time you had to make a decision with incomplete information.
text:
In the second week of April 2020, I had to decide whether to stop all fresh disbursements across our 140 branches. We had ₹380 crore of sanctioned but undisbursed home loans in the pipeline, and no idea how long the lockdown would last or how many of our customers would lose income.

I decided to pause all disbursements except for under-construction cases where stopping would leave the customer with a half-built house and us with weaker security. That was about ₹95 crore. We held the rest for six weeks and then reassessed each case, rejecting about 12% after fresh income checks.

Some customers were upset, and two builder partners complained loudly. But it protected our liquidity at a time when collections had dropped by nearly half. What I learned was that waiting for perfect information is itself a decision, usually a bad one, and that a clear rule with a narrow exception works better than case-by-case judgement in a crisis.

prompt: How do you handle fraud risk in retail lending?
text:
Fraud in retail lending comes in many forms. A customer may use fake documents. Someone may use another person's identity. A sales agent or DSA may create false files. Sometimes our own staff are involved. Each type needs a different control.

I think about fraud control in three stages.

Before the loan, we check identity and documents carefully. We use e-KYC and video KYC. We check PAN and Aadhaar details against official databases. We verify income documents at the source where possible, for example by pulling bank statements directly through the Account Aggregator system rather than accepting PDFs. We also run each application through a fraud check tool that looks for patterns, such as the same phone number or address appearing in many applications.

At the time of the loan, we make sure money goes only to the right account. We do field visits on a sample basis and for higher-risk cases. We check that the property or vehicle actually exists.

After the loan, we watch for early warning signs. A loan that never pays its first EMI is often a fraud case. We trace such cases back to the sourcing agent, branch and staff. If a pattern shows up, we stop business with that source and investigate.

We also report fraud cases to the RBI as required and share information through industry databases. Finally, we train our staff to spot fraud and give them a safe way to report it, including against their own colleagues.

prompt: How would you improve customer experience in a lending business?
text:
Start by actually going through it yourself. I know that sounds obvious, but it's amazing how few senior people in lending have ever applied for a loan at their own company as a regular customer. A few years back, I had a cousin apply for a home loan with us without telling anyone she was related to me. She sent me a running WhatsApp commentary. It was humbling.

She had to submit her salary slips three times, because each team asked for them separately. Nobody told her what the processing fee was until the sanction letter. Her relationship manager changed halfway through. The valuation visit got rescheduled twice and nobody called to say so. Total time from application to disbursement was 26 days. None of it was dramatic, but all of it added up to 'this company doesn't really care.'

So my answer to how you improve customer experience is mostly: fix the boring stuff that annoys people.

Ask for each document once. Build the system so that whatever's uploaded is visible to everyone who needs it. Tell people what things cost upfront, in rupees, not buried in a schedule of charges. Give them one person who owns their case till disbursement. Send an update when something changes, especially when it's a delay. And make it easy to reach a human when they need one.

After disbursement, the experience mostly lives in servicing and collections. Can they get a statement or a foreclosure letter without visiting the branch? When they call, does someone answer? If they miss an EMI, is the first call respectful? Those moments shape how people talk about you far more than your onboarding app does.

And measure it honestly. NPS is fine, but I'd look at complaints, repeat calls and how many people drop off at each stage. Those numbers don't lie as easily.

Oh, and my cousin did get the loan. She also got the processing fee waived, after I quietly fixed things. Which, of course, proves the point. Most customers don't have a cousin to call.

prompt: How do you manage relationships with credit rating agencies?
text:
For any NBFC or HFC, the credit rating is one of the most important determinants of its cost and availability of funds. A single notch upgrade, say from AA- to AA, can bring down the borrowing cost by 25 to 40 basis points and also open up access to a larger pool of investors such as insurance companies and pension funds, many of whom have internal restrictions on investing below a particular rating. Similarly, a downgrade can have a cascading effect on funding. Hence, managing the relationship with rating agencies like CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings and Acuité is a key responsibility of the CFO and the MD.

In my view, the foundation of a good relationship with the rating agency is transparency and consistency. Rating analysts are experienced professionals and they look at the same set of data across many institutions. Any attempt to present a selective picture will eventually come to light and damage credibility. It is always better to share both good and bad news proactively, along with the management's plan to address the issues.

Secondly, the communication should not be limited to the annual surveillance meeting. We follow the practice of sharing quarterly updates on key parameters such as AUM growth, asset quality, collection efficiency, ALM position, capital adequacy and liquidity buffer, even when the same is not specifically asked for. Any material event, whether it is a large fresh borrowing, a change in senior management, a significant regulatory development or a spike in delinquency in any particular segment, should be intimated to the agency at the earliest.

Thirdly, the management should understand the rating methodology of each agency in detail. Each agency publishes its criteria for NBFCs, covering parameters like parentage, market position, capitalisation, asset quality, earnings, liquidity and governance. Knowing these helps the management to identify the areas which are holding back the rating and work on the same in a focused manner.

Fourthly, senior management involvement is very important. The rating committee wants to hear the strategy directly from the MD and CFO, and not only from the treasury team. Questions on business plan, risk appetite and governance practices are best answered by the top management itself.

Lastly, the NBFC should always maintain an arm's length relationship. As per SEBI regulations, there are strict norms on rating shopping and on non-cooperation with rating agencies. The objective is to build trust and credibility over time, so that the agency has full comfort with the information provided and with the management's track record of delivering on what it commits.

prompt: Case: Your NBFC's cost of funds has risen by 120 basis points in a year. How do you respond?
text:
A 120 basis point increase in cost of funds within a year is a significant shock for any NBFC, since it can wipe out a large share of net interest margin if not addressed. The right response depends on why it has happened, how much of the asset book can absorb a repricing, and how quickly the liability side can be restructured. I would approach it in four steps.

First, diagnose the cause. A rise in cost of funds can stem from systemic factors, such as an RBI rate hiking cycle or tighter liquidity conditions, or from institution-specific factors, such as a rating downgrade, concerns about asset quality, or excessive dependence on a funding source that has become more expensive. In practice, it is often a combination. If the broader market has seen rates rise by, say, 80 to 100 basis points while our increase is 120, the additional 20 to 40 basis points signals an institution-specific premium that needs separate attention. The mix of borrowings matters too: a book heavily linked to bank MCLR or repo rates will reprice quickly, while long-term fixed-rate NCDs will reprice only as they mature.

Second, protect the margin through asset-side actions. The ability to pass on the increase depends on the product mix. Floating-rate loans linked to an internal benchmark can be repriced, though lenders should communicate clearly and fairly with borrowers, consistent with RBI guidance on the reset of floating rates, including offering options to increase tenure or EMI or to switch to a fixed rate. Fixed-rate products such as vehicle loans or personal loans can only be repriced for new disbursements. A useful exercise is to calculate the weighted repricing gap and estimate how much of the 120 basis points can be passed through over the next four quarters, and how much margin compression is unavoidable. At the same time, the business should review whether the product mix should tilt towards higher-yielding segments, though this must be done carefully to avoid simply taking on more credit risk to compensate.

Third, work on the liability side. Options include diversifying away from the most expensive sources, increasing securitisation and direct assignment of high-quality pools, which are priced on the strength of the underlying assets rather than the NBFC's own rating, exploring co-lending to reduce on-balance-sheet funding needs, and accessing refinance from NHB or SIDBI where eligible. Larger NBFCs may also consider external commercial borrowings with appropriate hedging. If an institution-specific premium is a factor, engaging proactively with lenders and rating agencies to address their concerns, through better disclosure, capital raising or demonstrable improvement in asset quality, can narrow the spread over time.

Fourth, look at operating costs. If margins will compress even after repricing, efficiency gains can offset part of the impact. Digitising processes, rationalising underperforming branches and improving collection efficiency to reduce credit costs all help protect return on assets.

Throughout, communication matters. The board should receive a clear analysis of the impact on profitability under different scenarios, along with the action plan. Investors and lenders should hear a coherent narrative rather than piecemeal explanations.

The key strategic lesson is that such shocks expose structural vulnerabilities. If the NBFC had a concentrated, short-tenor or rate-sensitive borrowing profile, the episode should prompt lasting changes to its funding strategy, so that the next cycle has a smaller impact.

prompt: Discuss the opportunities and risks in supply chain and dealer finance for NBFCs.
text:
Supply chain finance encompasses a range of financing arrangements that leverage the commercial relationships between a large corporate, commonly referred to as the anchor, and the smaller enterprises that supply to it or distribute its products. In the Indian context, the principal forms include dealer or distributor finance, in which working capital is extended to the anchor's downstream partners for the purchase of inventory, and vendor or supplier finance, in which upstream suppliers receive early payment against invoices raised on the anchor. For non-banking financial companies, the segment presents significant opportunities, but it also carries distinctive risks that require careful management.

The opportunities are substantial. India's micro, small and medium enterprises face a well-documented working capital gap, owing in large part to extended payment cycles from large buyers and limited access to collateral-free bank credit. Supply chain finance addresses this gap by drawing upon the credit strength of the anchor and the transactional history between the anchor and its partners, thereby enabling financing to enterprises that might not qualify for credit on a standalone basis. For the lender, the anchor relationship provides a cost-efficient channel for customer acquisition, access to reliable data on purchase and payment behaviour and, in many structures, a degree of comfort through the anchor's involvement in the arrangement.

Digital infrastructure has further expanded the opportunity. The integration of lending platforms with the anchor's enterprise resource planning systems, the availability of GST invoice data and the growth of the Trade Receivables Discounting System have reduced documentation requirements and the cost of processing small-value transactions. The segment also offers favourable portfolio characteristics. Tenors are short, typically ranging from thirty to one hundred and twenty days, which supports asset-liability matching and permits rapid repricing. The self-liquidating nature of trade transactions, in which repayment is linked to the sale of goods or the settlement of invoices, provides a natural source of repayment.

These opportunities are, however, accompanied by material risks.

The first is concentration risk. Exposure in supply chain programmes is often concentrated around a limited number of anchors and sectors. A deterioration in the anchor's business, or a downturn in the sector, can affect a large number of borrowers simultaneously. Prudent institutions therefore establish limits on exposure linked to any single anchor, sector or geography.

The second is the risk of over-reliance on the anchor. Lenders sometimes assume that the anchor will absorb losses or compel its partners to repay, when the underlying documentation may provide only limited recourse or none at all. The precise nature of any anchor commitment, whether a first-loss guarantee, a stop-supply arrangement or merely a referral, must be clearly understood and reflected in underwriting and pricing.

The third is fraud and the diversion of funds. Supply chain finance is vulnerable to fictitious invoices, duplicate financing of the same invoice by multiple lenders, and diversion of funds for purposes unrelated to the underlying trade. Verification of invoices against GST data and anchor records, together with registration on platforms that prevent duplicate financing, are essential controls.

The fourth is operational risk. The volume and velocity of transactions place considerable demands on systems for limit management, disbursement, reconciliation and collection. Weak operational controls can result in exposures exceeding approved limits or in the delayed identification of overdue accounts.

The fifth is the risk of evergreening. Because facilities are revolving, a borrower in difficulty may continue to draw and repay in a manner that masks underlying stress. Monitoring should therefore focus on utilisation patterns, the ageing of individual tranches and the borrower's broader financial position, rather than on overdue status alone.

In conclusion, supply chain and dealer finance offers NBFCs an attractive avenue for growth in MSME lending, combining short tenors, data-rich underwriting and efficient customer acquisition. Realising this potential, however, requires disciplined anchor selection, a clear understanding of contractual protections, robust fraud controls and sophisticated monitoring.

prompt: Case: A large DSA partner is found to be submitting fabricated documents. What do you do?
text:
We faced exactly this in August 2023. One of our top ten DSAs in Pune, contributing about ₹22 crore a month in home loan logins, was found to be submitting salary slips and Form 16s that had been altered. Our post-disbursement review team caught it when four loans from the same DSA bounced on the very first EMI.

I froze all fresh logins from that DSA the same day and stopped disbursement on 61 files in the pipeline. We then re-verified every live loan sourced by them over the previous 18 months, about 640 accounts worth roughly ₹190 crore. Around 9% had material discrepancies. For those customers, we did fresh income assessments and in some cases recalled the loan or sought additional security.

We terminated the DSA, filed a police complaint, reported the fraud to the RBI as required, and shared the details with the industry through the appropriate channels. Two of our own sales staff who had ignored warning signs faced disciplinary action.

The bigger fix was preventive. We now pull bank statements through the Account Aggregator for salaried customers and track first-EMI bounces by DSA every week.

prompt: What KPIs would you track as head of collections?
text:
As head of collections, I would track a small set of numbers that tell me three things: how much money we are collecting, how well we are stopping accounts from getting worse, and whether we are treating customers properly.

For collection performance, the first number is collection efficiency. This is the amount collected in a month divided by the amount due. I would look at it with and without arrears, because including old dues can hide a weak current month. I would also track the bounce rate, which is the share of EMIs that fail on the due date.

For movement between buckets, I would track roll rates. This means the share of accounts that move from one overdue bucket to the next, for example from 1-30 days to 31-60 days. I would also track the cure rate, which is the share that go back to paying normally. Roll rates are the clearest early sign of trouble. If more accounts are rolling forward this month than last month, I need to act now.

For bad loans, I would track the gross NPA ratio, new slippages into NPA, and recoveries from accounts that have already gone bad, including through SARFAESI and settlements.

For efficiency, I would look at the cost of collection per rupee collected, the number of accounts handled per collector, and how many promises to pay are actually kept.

For customer treatment, I would track complaints about collection staff, especially complaints to the RBI Ombudsman, and the results of audits of call recordings. A collector with great numbers but many complaints is a risk, not a star.

I would review these by branch, product, agency and individual. Averages can hide problems, so the detail matters.

prompt: How would you design incentive structures for a sales team without compromising credit quality?
text:
Okay, so I'll admit I learned this one by getting it wrong first.

Early in my time running a home loan business, our sales incentive was simple: you got paid on disbursement volume. More rupees out the door, bigger payout. It worked brilliantly, in the sense that disbursements went up 40% in a year. It also worked terribly, in the sense that about eighteen months later, the loans from our top-performing salespeople were bouncing at nearly twice the rate of everyone else's. We'd basically paid people to bring in risk.

The fix isn't to stop paying for volume. Sales teams need to sell, and if you make the incentive too complicated or too dependent on things they can't control, they'll stop caring about it. What we ended up with had three bits.

The biggest chunk, around 60-65%, was still linked to disbursements. But only for files that cleared credit without major deviations. If a file needed a big exception to get through, it counted for less.

Then about 25% depended on how the person's loans were performing. We used early indicators, mainly first-EMI and first-six-months bounce rates, because waiting two years to see if a loan goes NPA is useless for an incentive. If your bounce rate was well above the branch average, that portion shrank. If it was low, it grew a little.

The last bit, maybe 10-15%, was a deferred component that got paid out after a year, and could be clawed back if there was fraud or serious misrepresentation in files you'd sourced. That one made people pay attention to who they were working with, especially DSAs.

A couple of things made it actually work. We showed people their numbers every week on their phones, so nobody was surprised at the end of the quarter. And managers' incentives followed the same logic, which mattered more than I expected. If the branch manager's only paid on volume, he'll lean on the team no matter what their own scheme says.

Did volumes dip? A bit, for one quarter. Then they came back, and the quality was much better. A few of our 'star' salespeople left, and honestly, that was fine.

prompt: What is your approach to cross-selling insurance and other products to borrowers?
text:
Cross-selling of insurance and other third-party products is an important source of fee income for NBFCs and HFCs, and if done properly it also adds genuine value for the customer. For instance, a credit life insurance policy ensures that in the unfortunate event of the borrower's demise, the outstanding loan is repaid by the insurer and the family does not lose the house. Similarly, property insurance, health insurance and motor insurance are relevant for different customer segments. In many cases, our customers in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns do not have any insurance coverage at all, and hence there is a real need.

However, I must say that the industry's track record in this area has not been very good. Mis-selling has been a serious concern, and both the RBI and IRDAI have expressed their displeasure on this matter several times. Common issues include bundling of insurance with the loan without the customer's informed consent, deducting the premium from the loan amount without proper explanation, selling policies which are not suitable for the customer's needs, and forcing customers to buy insurance from a particular insurer as a condition for sanction of the loan. There have also been complaints of customers not receiving the policy document at all, and of claims being rejected on technical grounds.

In our organisation, we follow a few basic principles in this regard.

Firstly, insurance is always optional, and the same is clearly communicated to the customer both verbally and in writing. The loan sanction is never linked to the purchase of any insurance product, except where the loan product itself requires the asset to be insured, and even in that case the customer is free to choose the insurer.

Secondly, the premium amount, coverage, tenure and key exclusions are explained to the customer in his own language before he signs. The premium is shown separately in the key fact statement and in the disbursement breakup.

Thirdly, the policy document is delivered to the customer within a defined timeline, and our branch staff are trained to assist the family at the time of a claim. We track the claim settlement ratios and turnaround time of our insurance partners closely.

Fourthly, sales incentives on cross-sell are kept moderate, and we monitor penetration rates by branch and employee. An unusually high penetration in any branch is treated as a red flag and is checked through customer calling.

Lastly, we take customer feedback seriously. Any complaint regarding forced or mis-sold insurance is investigated, and where the complaint is found to be genuine, the premium is refunded and suitable action is taken against the concerned employee.

In my view, cross-selling done with integrity strengthens the relationship with the customer. Done wrongly, it damages trust and invites regulatory action, which is simply not worth the fee income.

prompt: How can a lending company integrate ESG into its business?
text:
For a lending company, ESG is often discussed mainly in terms of disclosures and ratings, but its real significance lies in how environmental, social and governance factors affect credit risk, customer outcomes and the long-term sustainability of the business. Integrating ESG well means embedding it into strategy, underwriting and operations rather than treating it as a separate reporting exercise.

On the environmental side, the most significant impact of a lending company comes through the activities it finances, not its own operations. A good starting point is to understand the climate and environmental exposure of the loan book. For an Indian NBFC, this might include the vulnerability of agricultural or rural borrowers to droughts and floods, the concentration of MSME borrowers in polluting industries that may face tighter regulation, or the location of mortgaged properties in flood-prone areas. The RBI has published a draft disclosure framework on climate-related financial risks and has encouraged regulated entities to begin assessing these risks, so building internal capability now is prudent. At the same time, there are opportunities in green finance, such as loans for electric vehicles, rooftop solar, energy-efficient housing and green buildings. Several NBFCs have launched dedicated EV financing products, and green bonds offer a way to access investors focused on sustainable finance.

The social dimension is particularly important in Indian lending. Financial inclusion is a core social contribution of many NBFCs, which serve customers in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns, women borrowers, MSMEs and new-to-credit households that banks often do not reach. But social responsibility also means responsible lending: avoiding over-indebtedness, ensuring transparent pricing, preventing mis-selling of insurance and other products, and maintaining fair and respectful collection practices. The experience of the microfinance sector during periods of stress, and the concerns about aggressive digital lending apps, show how quickly poor practices can harm customers and damage the reputation of the entire industry. Measuring outcomes such as complaint rates, grievance resolution times and the share of loans to women or first-time borrowers helps make this concrete. Internally, social factors include employee safety, fair pay and working conditions for field staff, and diversity across the workforce.

Governance is the foundation. This covers board independence and competence, robust risk management, effective internal controls, transparent related party transactions, data privacy and protection, and a culture of compliance. The RBI's scale-based regulation framework has raised governance expectations for larger NBFCs, and listed entities among the top 1,000 by market capitalisation are required by SEBI to publish a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. Strong governance is also what investors, lenders and rating agencies look at most closely when assessing an NBFC.

To integrate ESG effectively, a lending company can take several practical steps. It can adopt a board-approved ESG policy with clear objectives and accountability at the senior management level. It can build an exclusion list of activities it will not finance and incorporate ESG screening into credit appraisal for larger or higher-risk exposures. It can set measurable targets, for example on the share of green loans, financial inclusion reach or customer complaint rates, and link them to management performance assessment. And it can disclose progress transparently, including areas where it has fallen short.

The business case is increasingly clear. Development finance institutions and many international lenders now prefer, or require, borrowers to demonstrate credible ESG practices, which can provide access to longer-tenor and sometimes cheaper funding. Customers and employees increasingly value responsible institutions. And many ESG risks, from climate events to conduct failures, are ultimately credit and reputational risks that a well-managed lender would want to understand and mitigate in any case.

prompt: How do you manage relationships with DSAs while controlling sourcing quality?
text:
Direct selling agents remain a significant source of business for most retail lenders in India, and the relationship must be managed so as to secure volume without compromising credit quality or conduct standards.

The foundation is rigorous empanelment, including verification of the agent's background, financial standing and track record, together with a written agreement that sets out responsibilities, the code of conduct and the consequences of misrepresentation. Under the Reserve Bank of India's outsourcing guidelines, the lender remains accountable for the conduct of its agents.

Thereafter, performance should be assessed on quality as well as quantity. Metrics such as login-to-sanction ratios, deviation rates, early delinquency on sourced loans and detected fraud should be reviewed regularly and should influence payouts. Credit decisions must remain entirely independent of the DSA.

Finally, periodic audits, customer verification calls and training sessions help sustain standards, while the prompt termination of non-compliant agents reinforces the institution's expectations across the network. Payout structures should, moreover, avoid rewarding volume in isolation.

prompt: How do you communicate bad news to the board?
text:
Early, in person if possible, and with numbers. In Q3 of FY2023-24, early delinquencies in our small business loan portfolio jumped sharply. The 30+ DPD on loans disbursed in the previous nine months went from 2.4% to 4.1% in a single quarter, on a book of about ₹2,600 crore. It was not yet visible in our GNPA, and the next board meeting was seven weeks away.

I called our chairman and the chair of the Risk Management Committee within a week of seeing the data, before we fully understood the cause. I told them what we knew, what we did not know, and when I expected to have answers. Some colleagues felt we should wait until we had a complete diagnosis. I disagreed. In my experience, boards can handle bad news. What they do not forgive is finding out late.

At the board meeting, I presented a short note: what had happened, the likely causes (about 70% of the slippage came from two states and three sourcing channels), the actions already taken, including a 30% cut in sourcing from those channels, and a range of possible outcomes for credit cost, from ₹38 crore to ₹65 crore over the next year. I did not soften the language or bury the numbers in an annexure.

I also took responsibility. Board members respect accountability far more than explanations. By the end of FY2024-25, the cohort had stabilised and the credit cost came in at ₹49 crore. More importantly, the board's trust in management was stronger than before.
