prompt: How should lenders treat vulnerable customers and ensure fair practices?
text:
Some borrowers are more likely to be harmed by a loan than others. They may be elderly, sick, recently bereaved, or have lost a job. They may not read well, or may not understand financial terms. They may be in a crisis and willing to sign anything to get money quickly. A good lender takes extra care with such customers.

The RBI's Fair Practices Code sets the base rules for all NBFCs. Lenders must give clear information about the loan in a language the customer understands. They must share a key fact statement with the full cost of the loan. They must give reasons if they reject an application. They must not change terms without notice. They must not use harsh methods to collect dues. These rules apply to everyone, but they matter most for vulnerable customers.

Beyond the rules, I think lenders should do a few more things.

First, train frontline staff to notice signs of vulnerability. A customer who seems confused, who is being pushed by someone else, or who is borrowing to repay another loan needs a slower conversation.

Second, check if the loan is affordable. Do not lend just because the customer has collateral. If the EMI will leave the family short of money for food or school fees, the loan is likely to cause harm.

Third, keep the product simple. Avoid complex fees and add-ons. Do not bundle insurance without clear consent.

Fourth, be flexible when problems happen. If a borrower falls ill or loses income, talk to them. Offer options such as a longer tenure or a short break where policy allows.

Fifth, make collections humane. No calls at odd hours. No threats. No pressure on family members. Monitor agents and act when they break the rules.

Finally, make it easy to complain. Have a simple process, respond quickly, and look for patterns in complaints.

Treating vulnerable customers fairly is the right thing to do. It also protects the lender from losses, regulatory action and damage to its name.

prompt: How do you think about microfinance and the risk of over-indebtedness?
text:
I've got a slightly complicated relationship with microfinance, if I'm being honest. I've seen it do real good. I've also seen it go badly wrong, sometimes in the same district a few years apart.

The good side is easy to forget if you only read the headlines. When I first visited a joint liability group meeting in a village near Gaya, maybe fifteen years ago, there were women there who'd never had a bank account, never had a loan from anyone except a moneylender charging 5% a month. One of them had started selling saris from home with a ₹15,000 loan and was on her third cycle. She was proud of it, and she had every reason to be.

The bad side is what happens when too many lenders chase the same borrowers. I've watched it play out more than once. Growth is strong, collections look great at 99%, everyone's expanding, new players come in. Then one day you realise the woman who had one loan now has four, from four different lenders, and she's paying the third with money from the fourth. The collection numbers stay perfect right up until they don't. Andhra Pradesh in 2010 was the extreme version. Parts of Bihar, Jharkhand and a few other states have had milder versions more recently.

What's frustrating is that it's mostly preventable. RBI's 2022 framework actually got the principle right. It ties lending to household income and caps total repayments at 50% of monthly household income, across all lenders. The problem is that measuring income for these households is genuinely hard, and there's always a temptation to be generous with the estimate when you've got targets. The industry's own guardrails, limiting the number of lenders per borrower, came in a bit late, but they help.

If I were running a microfinance book today, I'd care much more about the number of active lenders per borrower and total household debt in the bureau than about my own collection rate. Collection efficiency's a lagging indicator in microfinance. By the time it drops, the damage is done.

I'd also slow down in districts where credit has grown too fast, even if it means losing share. That's a hard conversation to have with a board, but it's a lot easier than explaining a 15% write-off two years later.

And frankly, I'd spend time in group meetings. Not reviews, actual meetings. You learn more about over-indebtedness from twenty minutes of listening than from any dashboard.

prompt: How would you use a SWOT analysis when your NBFC is entering a new state?
text:
SWOT analysis is a simple but effective tool to structure the thinking before entering a new geography. In my experience, the value of the exercise lies not in filling the four boxes but in honestly assessing whether the company's strengths are actually relevant to the new market. Let me take the example of an affordable housing and LAP focused NBFC, presently operating in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, which is evaluating entry into Rajasthan.

Coming to Strengths first, the company would list its capabilities such as proven underwriting of self-employed and informal income customers, an established technology platform for loan origination, reasonably good brand recall in neighbouring regions, a stable funding profile with a good credit rating, and an experienced management team. The key question here is which of these strengths will travel. For instance, the underwriting model may have been built on the business patterns of traders in Gujarat, and the same may need modification for the agrarian and handicraft-based economy in many parts of Rajasthan.

Weaknesses would include lack of local market knowledge, no existing relationships with DSAs, builders and lawyers in the state, absence of local language and cultural familiarity among the present team, and unfamiliarity with the state-specific land records and property registration system. The company should be candid here, as these are precisely the areas where mistakes happen in the first two years.

Opportunities in Rajasthan are considerable. The state has a large and growing number of Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns such as Bhilwara, Sikar, Alwar, Kota and Bikaner, with a significant population of small business owners and self-employed individuals who are underserved by banks. Housing demand is strong, the state government has taken several steps towards digitisation of land records, and overall credit penetration is lower than the national average. There may also be scope to partner with banks under co-lending, since banks require PSL-eligible assets from such regions.

Threats would include intense competition from existing affordable housing finance companies and small finance banks which are already well entrenched, the risk of hiring mis-sellers or poor quality staff in a hurry, variability in monsoon and its impact on rural incomes, and concentration risk if the initial branches are set up in towns with a single dominant industry. Regulatory or political risk at the state level, such as loan waiver announcements or local agitations, should also be considered.

Once the SWOT is done, the next step is to convert it into an action plan. Strengths should be leveraged for differentiation, weaknesses should be addressed through hiring of local senior talent and building legal and technical panels before launch, opportunities should be prioritised by selecting the right first set of towns, and threats should be mitigated through prudent credit policy and exposure limits. In our case, we would recommend a phased entry, starting with eight to ten branches in a cluster, and scaling up only after reviewing the portfolio performance after 12 to 18 months.

Kindly note that SWOT is only a starting point and should be supplemented with detailed market sizing, competitor benchmarking and unit economics analysis before final board approval.

prompt: How do you manage a merger or integration of two lending businesses?
text:
Mergers in lending are difficult to execute well because they combine two balance sheets, two sets of customers, two cultures and two technology stacks in a business where small errors in data or process can quickly become credit, regulatory or reputational problems. Indian financial services has seen several large integrations in recent years, including bank-NBFC mergers and consolidation among HFCs and NBFCs, and that experience points to a few principles that matter most.

The first is clarity on the strategic rationale, communicated consistently. Is the merger primarily about scale, access to lower-cost funding, geographic expansion, product diversification or regulatory requirements? The answer should shape every subsequent decision, from which products are retained to which technology platform survives. If the rationale is unclear, integration decisions become negotiations between the two organisations rather than choices made in the interest of the combined entity.

The second is rigorous due diligence on the loan book, which continues after the deal is signed. Underwriting standards, collection practices, restructured accounts, provisioning methodologies and the quality of documentation can differ significantly between the two entities. Harmonising ECL methodologies and asset classification, especially if one entity is a bank following IRACP norms and the other an NBFC, often leads to a revision of reported asset quality. It is better to identify and disclose such differences early than to be surprised a few quarters later.

The third is regulatory and legal planning. A merger involving regulated entities requires approvals from the RBI and, depending on the structure, from the NCLT, the Competition Commission of India, SEBI and the stock exchanges. Each approval has its own timeline and conditions. Where an NBFC merges into a bank, there are additional complexities, such as meeting priority sector lending targets on the enlarged book, maintaining CRR and SLR on liabilities that were previously not subject to them, and aligning products and practices with banking regulations. These have material financial implications and should be planned in detail before the merger becomes effective.

The fourth is people and culture. In most integrations, the biggest risk is the loss of key talent and the disengagement of frontline staff during a prolonged period of uncertainty. Leaders should decide the senior leadership structure quickly, communicate openly about which roles will change and when, and treat employees from both organisations fairly. Cultural differences, for instance between a fast-moving, entrepreneurial NBFC and a process-driven bank, are real and should be acknowledged rather than wished away. Joint teams, shared objectives and visible leadership from both sides help build a common identity.

The fifth is technology and data integration. Migrating loan accounts to a single core platform is one of the highest-risk activities in any lending merger. Data mapping, reconciliation of balances and charges, and mock migrations need sufficient time. Customers should not experience errors in their EMIs, statements or bureau reporting, which can quickly lead to complaints and regulatory scrutiny. A phased approach, with the most critical systems integrated first, is often safer than a single big-bang cutover.

The sixth is customer continuity. Customers of the acquired entity should be told clearly what will change, such as account numbers, payment methods, branch locations or interest rate benchmarks, and what will not. Any change in terms must be handled carefully and in line with fair practices requirements. Relationship managers, DSAs and builder partners also need clear communication to avoid business leaking to competitors.

Finally, the governance of the integration itself matters. A dedicated integration management office, a steering committee chaired by the CEO, clear milestones and regular board reporting help maintain momentum and accountability. Synergy targets should be realistic and tracked, with honest reporting when they slip.

Integrations that succeed usually combine decisive leadership on the big questions with patience and care on the details. Those that struggle typically underestimate the time required, overestimate the synergies, and neglect the people who have to make the combined business work.

prompt: How would you build a customer-centric culture in a branch network?
text:
A customer-centric culture in a branch network cannot be created through slogans or training programmes alone; it must be reflected in the incentives, processes and daily behaviours of every branch.

The first requirement is that leadership defines, in practical terms, what good customer treatment looks like. This includes standards for turnaround time, clarity of communication regarding costs and terms, responsiveness to queries and respectful conduct during collections.

The second requirement is measurement. Branch performance should be assessed not only on disbursements and collections but also on complaint incidence, resolution timelines, customer feedback scores and the findings of mystery shopping exercises. These metrics should carry genuine weight in performance appraisal and incentives.

The third requirement is empowerment. Branch managers should have the authority to resolve routine customer issues, such as fee reversals or documentation errors, without lengthy escalation.

Finally, senior management must model the desired behaviour. Regular branch visits that include conversations with customers, the review of complaint data at management committee meetings and the visible recognition of employees who demonstrate exceptional service all signal that customer centricity is an organisational priority rather than an aspiration.

prompt: How do you mentor and develop future leaders in your organisation?
text:
I spend roughly 15% of my time on this, and I block it in the calendar because otherwise it gets eaten up by everything else.

At any point, I personally mentor about eight people, usually regional heads, product heads and a couple of high-potential managers a level below. I meet each of them once a month for an hour, outside the formal review process. These conversations are not about their targets. We talk about decisions they are struggling with, people issues, and what they want to be doing in five years.

The most useful thing I do, I think, is give people stretch roles before they feel fully ready. In FY2022-23, I moved our 34-year-old head of collections for the West zone to run our new MSME business, which had a book of just ₹180 crore at the time. Several people thought it was a risk. She had never run a P&L. But she understood risk deeply, and that business needed someone who would build it carefully. The book crossed ₹1,100 crore in two years with GNPA under 1.5%.

I also try to make sure leaders get exposure across functions. Our succession plan requires that anyone considered for a business head role has spent time in at least two of credit, collections and operations, in addition to sales.

We formalised this two years ago into a leadership programme for about 40 people a year, with an external partner for some modules, but much of the learning still comes from projects and rotations.

The measure I care about is simple: of our top 25 roles, how many could be filled internally tomorrow? In FY2021-22 it was 9. Today it is 17.

prompt: How do you approach vehicle finance in rural markets?
text:
Vehicle finance in rural India is a large and steady business. Farmers buy tractors. Small transporters buy pickup trucks. Young people buy two-wheelers to get to work or college. Many of these buyers have no salary slip and no income tax return. Banks often find them hard to serve. NBFCs have built a strong business by learning how to lend to them.

My approach rests on a few simple ideas.

First, know the customer's income. For a farmer, income depends on the crop, the land size, irrigation and the market price. For a small transporter, it depends on how many days the vehicle runs and what it carries. Our field staff must visit the customer, see the land or the business, and make a fair estimate of what the family earns. We also look at bank statements and bureau records where available.

Second, match the repayment to the income. A farmer earns most of his money after harvest. A monthly EMI may not suit him. Quarterly or half-yearly repayments, timed to the crop cycle, work better and reduce defaults.

Third, work closely with dealers. Most customers come through dealers. Good dealers bring good customers. We track loan performance by dealer and stop working with those whose customers default often or whose files have problems.

Fourth, keep the down payment and loan size sensible. A larger down payment means the customer has more at stake. It also protects us if the vehicle has to be repossessed and sold.

Fifth, be careful with repossession. It is sometimes needed, but it must follow the law and the RBI's rules. Customers must get proper notice. Agents must behave properly. Taking away a farmer's tractor during the sowing season can ruin a family, so it should be the last step, not the first.

Sixth, watch the weather and the economy. A poor monsoon or a fall in crop prices can hit many customers at once. We should spread our lending across districts and crops, and be ready to give relief when there is a genuine crisis.

Done this way, rural vehicle finance can grow steadily with manageable losses, and it helps families earn more and live better.

prompt: Case: You're launching an EV two-wheeler loan product. What would your go-to-market be?
text:
I'd start smaller than the marketing team would like. Probably a lot smaller.

The thing with EV two-wheelers is that the credit risk isn't quite the same as a petrol scooter, and a fair few lenders found that out the expensive way. Resale value is the big unknown. With a Honda Activa, you know roughly what a three-year-old one will fetch, and so does every repo yard in the country. With an electric scooter from a brand that's been around four years, maybe it's ₹40,000, maybe it's ₹15,000 because the battery's degraded and the company's changed its model twice. Some brands have had service networks collapse. A couple went under. So your recovery assumptions, which sit underneath your LTV and pricing, are shakier.

Given that, here's roughly how I'd approach it.

Pick the OEMs carefully. Two or three established manufacturers with decent service networks and some evidence on battery life, not every startup with a showroom. I'd also try to get some form of buyback or resale support from the OEM, or at least a battery warranty that transfers on repossession. That changes the LGD maths a lot.

Pick the customers carefully too. The obvious early segment is gig and delivery workers in cities, because the running-cost savings are real for them. Someone doing 80-100 km a day saves serious money on petrol. But their incomes are volatile, and many are new to credit. I'd want platform income data, ideally through tie-ups with the delivery companies, and I'd keep tickets modest. The other segment is salaried commuters in Tier 1 and the bigger Tier 2 cities, which is lower risk but more competitive.

Start in three or four cities where the OEMs have strong dealer networks and charging isn't a nightmare. Pune, Bengaluru, Jaipur, maybe Ahmedabad. Cap the pilot at something like ₹25-30 crore of disbursement, and run it for nine to twelve months before you scale.

Price it honestly. EV loans probably need a slightly higher rate than petrol two-wheelers until there's data, or a higher down payment. I wouldn't subsidise rates to grab share. That's the mistake I'd most want to avoid.

Think about the product a bit differently. Battery-as-a-service models, where the customer leases the battery separately, can lower the upfront cost and reduce the residual value problem for you. Worth exploring with OEMs who offer it.

Track things obsessively. Delinquency by OEM, by model, by dealer, by customer segment. And track repossession and resale outcomes, because that's where your assumptions get proven right or wrong.

And yes, there's a green story to tell, and some DFIs and impact investors will give you cheaper money for it. That's nice. But it doesn't change whether the loans get repaid. Get the credit right first. The ESG angle's a bonus.

prompt: What is your outlook for Indian NBFCs over the next five years?
text:
I am broadly optimistic about the outlook for Indian NBFCs over the next five years, although I believe the sector will look quite different from what it is today, and not all players will benefit equally.

The fundamental demand drivers remain very strong. India's credit-to-GDP ratio is still low compared to other major economies, and the household and MSME segments in particular are significantly under-penetrated. As per various estimates, the MSME credit gap itself is in the range of ₹20 to 25 lakh crore. Rising incomes, formalisation of the economy through GST and digital payments, and the aspirations of the young population in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns will continue to create demand for home loans, vehicle loans, gold loans, business loans and consumer credit. NBFCs, with their reach, agility and specialised underwriting skills, are well placed to serve these segments.

Secondly, the digital public infrastructure in India, namely Aadhaar-based e-KYC, UPI, the Account Aggregator framework, GSTN data and now the Unified Lending Interface being developed by the Reserve Bank Innovation Hub, has dramatically reduced the cost of acquiring and underwriting customers. NBFCs which leverage these effectively will be able to serve smaller ticket sizes profitably and reach new-to-credit customers at scale.

Thirdly, the regulatory framework has matured considerably. Post the IL&FS episode, the RBI has brought in scale-based regulation, liquidity coverage requirements, stricter NPA recognition norms and enhanced governance standards. While this has increased compliance costs, it has also strengthened the credibility of the sector with lenders and investors. The larger NBFCs are now regulated almost on par with banks.

However, there are certain challenges which the sector will have to deal with.

The first is funding. NBFCs continue to depend substantially on bank borrowings, and any change in the regulator's view on bank exposure to NBFCs, as we saw in November 2023, has a direct impact on cost and availability of funds. Diversification of the liability franchise through bonds, securitisation, co-lending and external borrowings will be critical.

The second is competition. Banks, especially the large private sector banks, are aggressively targeting the retail and MSME segments which were traditionally the domain of NBFCs. Small finance banks and fintech players are also competing for the same customers. NBFCs will need a clear right to win in their chosen segments, whether through superior customer knowledge, faster turnaround, or presence in geographies where banks are thin.

The third is asset quality in unsecured segments. The stress seen in microfinance and small-ticket personal loans during 2024 and 2025 is a reminder that credit cycles have not gone away. Lenders who had grown aggressively are now consolidating. Underwriting discipline will separate the winners from the rest.

The fourth is conduct and customer protection. The RBI has been very clear that it expects fair treatment of customers, especially in digital lending, collections and cross-selling. Any lapses in this regard may invite strict supervisory action, as we have seen in some cases recently.

Putting it all together, I expect the sector to continue growing at a healthy pace, perhaps in the range of 14% to 18% annually, with further consolidation. Well-governed, well-capitalised NBFCs with a clear niche and diversified funding will gain market share, while smaller players with weaker practices may find it difficult to survive or may get acquired. In my humble opinion, the next five years will reward discipline more than aggression.
